He looked tired—not physically, his immortal body could not experience fatigue, but there was a weariness in his eyes that I had never noticed before.*

*"Halvar," he said quietly. "Do you think I did the right thing?"*

*The question caught me completely off guard. "Your Majesty?"*

*"The Coalition. I could have let them be. I could have simply ignored their resistance, allowed them to maintain their philosophical independence. But I wanted to test my charisma. I was curious." He paused, his brow furrowing slightly. "Was that wrong of me? To strip them of their conviction, even if I replaced it with something better?"*

*I did not know how to answer. I still do not know. The King was genuinely asking my opinion, genuinely uncertain about the morality of his own actions. And I realized, with a chill that settled deep in my bones, that he was not asking because he was troubled. He was asking because he was curious. The question was just another experiment, another test of cause and effect. He was using me as a moral sounding board because he had lost the ability to perceive the ethical dimensions of his own power.*

*"I believe you acted appropriately, Your Majesty," I said, because it was the only answer I could give. It was the only answer my mind would allow me to give. The King's charisma, even in its passive, restrained state, made disagreement feel not merely impossible but unthinkable.*

*He smiled, patted my shoulder, and told me I was a good friend. And I felt warm. I felt loved. I felt valued. And beneath all of that, buried so deep I could barely perceive it, I felt the cold, gnawing certainty that my emotions were not entirely my own.*

*I am Halvar. I love my King. I fear my King. And I fear, most of all, that the love and the fear are the same thing, and that neither of them is truly mine.*

Kaedan closed the journal with trembling hands. The tears were streaming down his face now, hot and silent, dripping onto the leather cover and mingling with the ancient stains that marked its surface. He was crying for Unbroken Resolve, whose conviction had been so effortlessly overwritten. He was crying for Halvar, whose final confession had been so quietly devastating. He was crying for himself, because he knew—with absolute, terrifying certainty—that his own loyalty to the King was just as manufactured, just as inevitable, just as inescapable.

He reached for the final journal. His vision was blurred with tears, and he had to wipe his eyes repeatedly to make out the words on the spine. *Kael — Year 891,047 — Perception*.

---

**Year 891,047 — Kael — Perception**

*I am Kael. I am the most recent addition to this archive, though I know I will not be the last. The King's curiosity is inexhaustible, and his attributes are infinite. There will always be more tests, more demonstrations, more moments of cosmic horror that require recording.*

*My account concerns perception. Not sight, not hearing, not any of the mundane senses that mortal beings rely upon. Perception, in the context of the King's attributes, refers to his ability to perceive threats, intentions, possibilities, and outcomes. It is, in essence, the passive awareness that accompanies his omniscience—the mechanism through which he knows everything that has ever existed, could ever exist, or will ever exist.*

*The opposition in my account did not intend to fight the King. They intended to hide from him. They called themselves the Unseen, and they were a civilization that had dedicated billions of years to the mastery of concealment. They had developed technologies, magics, and conceptual frameworks that allowed them to exist entirely outside the perception of any known entity. They did not merely become invisible; they erased themselves from every possible detection matrix. They existed in the gaps between moments, in the spaces between thoughts, in the blind spots that exist at the intersection of all possible observational frameworks.*

*They believed, with the absolute confidence of beings who had never been perceived, that they could remain hidden from the King. They intended to build a civilization in the perceptual shadows of Thronegate itself, existing alongside the omniverse without ever being noticed.*

*They were wrong. They were so catastrophically wrong that I still struggle to articulate the horror of their mistake.*

*The King perceived them. He had perceived them from the moment their first ancestor conceived of the idea of concealment, billions of years before they achieved their goal. His perception stat, multiplying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for nearly nine hundred thousand years, was not constrained by the limitations of sensory input. It was an absolute, all-encompassing awareness that transcended the very concept of observation. He did not see the Unseen. He did not detect them. He simply knew them, with a completeness so total that their own self-awareness was merely a fragmentary subset of his understanding of them.*

*"They've been hiding from me for quite some time," the King said to me one afternoon, his tone as casual as if he were discussing the weather. "It's rather impressive, actually. Their concealment technology is genuinely innovative. I'm curious to see how they react when they realize it doesn't work."*

*He did not announce his awareness. He did not reveal himself to them. He simply... let them perceive him perceiving them.*

*I must pause here and explain what this meant. The King's perception was not passive. It was an active, penetrating force that, when directed at a target, did more than simply observe. It connected the observer and the observed in a loop of mutual awareness. When the King chose to truly perceive something, that thing could not help but perceive him right back.*

*So the Unseen, who had spent billions of years perfecting their concealment, suddenly found themselves perceiving the King. Not his physical form. Not his magical presence. They perceived his awareness of them. They felt, with the sudden, horrifying clarity of a lightning strike, that they were being watched. Not observed. Not detected. Watched. By an awareness so vast, so complete, so unimaginably penetrating that it made their own self-perception feel shallow and incomplete by comparison.*

*The psychological impact was immediate and catastrophic. The Unseen had built their entire civilization around the foundational premise that they could not be perceived. Their culture, their philosophy, their very sense of identity was predicated on their concealment. To suddenly perceive the King perceiving them was to have that foundational premise shattered in the most intimate, violating way possible.*

*I watched—through the King's perception, which he graciously shared with me—as the Unseen civilization collapsed into chaos. Some of them went mad instantly, their minds unable to reconcile the sudden, overwhelming awareness of being watched by an entity whose attention felt like the gaze of God. Others fell into catatonic states, their consciousness retreating inward in a desperate attempt to escape the King's perception. Still others became obsessed with the perception itself, devoting themselves to studying the exact nature of the awareness that had penetrated their concealment, spending the rest of their existence in a futile attempt to understand something that was fundamentally beyond their comprehension.*

*Their leader, a being who had perfected the art of nonexistence, experienced the most devastating fate. The King's perception was so complete, so penetrating, that it did not merely observe him—it understood him. It knew him down to his most fundamental essence, more completely than he had ever known himself. And in that knowledge, that absolute, total comprehension, the leader experienced an existential crisis from which he could never recover. He had defined himself by his ability to remain unseen. To be seen so completely, so utterly, was to have that identity destroyed. He did not die, but he ceased to exist as the person he had been. What remained was a hollow shell, a being who had been so thoroughly perceived that there was nothing left of his own self-conception.*

*The King watched all of this with an expression of mild, academic interest. He was not cruel about it. He did not gloat or savor their suffering. He was simply observing the results of his experiment, cataloging the data, filing it away in the infinite archives of his omniscience.*

*"Interesting," he said finally. "Their psychological dependence on concealment was much stronger than I anticipated. The feedback loop between perception and identity is a fascinating field of study."*

*He turned to me, and his expression shifted into that warm, fatherly smile that I have known since childhood. "Kael, you look troubled. Would you like to talk about it?"*

*I declined. I could not talk about it. I could barely process it. I had just witnessed an entire civilization be destroyed not by force or magic, but by the simple, passive fact of being perceived. The King had not attacked them. He had not threatened them. He had simply looked at them, truly looked at them, and that look had been enough to annihilate the very foundation of their existence.*

*I am Kael. I am the latest in a long line of Court Wizards who have had their understanding of reality shattered by witnessing the King's power. I love him. I fear him. And I know, with absolute certainty, that these journals will continue to be written for as long as the omniverse exists, because there is no end to the King's attributes, and there is no end to the horror of comprehending what he truly is.*

*May whoever reads this find some measure of peace in the knowledge that opposition is not merely futile—it is a privilege we are permitted only because the King is curious about how we will fail.*

---

Kaedan closed the final journal and sat in silence for a long, long time. The vault's amber lights pulsed with steady, indifferent rhythm. The scent of old paper and blood and ozone hung heavy in the temperate air. His tears had dried on his cheeks, leaving stiff, salty tracks that itched and pulled at his skin.

He understood now. He understood what his father had been trying to prepare him for. He understood why every Court Wizard before him had developed tremors in their hands and haunted flickers in their eyes. The King was not merely powerful. He was not merely omnipotent. He was a being whose every attribute, when expressed at even the smallest, most restrained fraction of its true magnitude, was sufficient to destroy the omniverse as a passive side effect. His strength could unmake reality through the simple fact of its existence. His speed rendered the concept of movement obsolete. His luck rewrote the mathematical foundations of chance. His charisma made resistance psychologically impossible. His perception was so complete that being seen by him was a form of existential annihilation.

And all of this—all of the horror, all of the destruction, all of the shattered civilizations and traumatized witnesses—was accomplished with effectively zero percent of his true power. The King had never exerted himself. He had never tried. He had simply allowed the faintest, most infinitesimal shadow of his attributes to express themselves, and the omniverse had shattered and reformed and been grateful for the privilege.

The door to the vault opened. Kaedan looked up, his eyes raw and swollen, and saw his father standing in the threshold. Corin's face was unreadable, but there was something in his posture—a softening of the shoulders, a slight release of tension—that suggested he understood exactly what his son was experiencing.

"You've finished," Corin said. It was not a question.

"Yes, Father."

"And?"

Kaedan opened his mouth to answer, but the words would not come. How could he possibly articulate what he had learned? How could he compress the accumulated horror of five eyewitness accounts—five generations of his own ancestors, each one traumatized in their own unique way—into a coherent response?

Corin nodded, as if the silence itself was answer enough. "You understand now why we write these journals. It is not for the King's benefit. He does not read them. He would not understand them if he did. He genuinely believes he is being restrained. He genuinely believes that using zero percent of his power is a courtesy. He cannot comprehend the scale of the gap between himself and the rest of creation. He has lost the ability to perceive it."

He stepped into the vault and placed a hand on his son's shoulder. The grip was gentle this time, no longer desperate or clawing.

"We write these journals for ourselves," Corin continued. "To process what we have witnessed. To maintain our sanity in the face of the incomprehensible. And we write them for you—for the next generation of Court Wizards who must understand what it means to serve a being whose slightest, most restrained action is an apocalyptic event for everyone else."

Kaedan looked down at the stack of journals, their leather covers stained with blood and tears and the accumulated dread of millennia. He thought about Zander, who had watched the King's passive strength unmake creation. He thought about Mirek, who had glimpsed what it meant to exist at every point in time simultaneously. He thought about Jovan, Halvar, and Kael, each of them shattered in their own way by the impossible magnitude of the King's attributes.

And he thought about the King himself—the warm, friendly, genuinely kind ruler who asked about his family and remembered his children's birthdays and laughed at his jokes. The man who had destroyed the entire omniverse multiple times through casual, passive expressions of his power, and who had restored it each time with zero effort and zero concern. The apex predator of all existence, whose love was as terrifying as his wrath, and whose curiosity was more dangerous than any weapon ever conceived.

"I understand, Father," Kaedan said quietly. "I understand that opposition is not merely futile. It is a mathematical impossibility that was disproven before the first atom of creation ever formed."

Corin nodded slowly. "Then you are ready to serve."

He turned and walked toward the vault exit, his silhouette framed by the dim light of the corridor beyond. Kaedan remained seated for a moment longer, staring at the journals that contained the accumulated trauma of his bloodline. He knew that he would add to this archive someday. He knew that he would witness something that would shatter his understanding of reality and leave him trembling and broken, and that he would record it here so that future generations would understand.

And he knew, with absolute, terrifying certainty, that he would continue to love the King regardless. Because that was the true horror of serving Godric of Thronegate. Not the power. Not the destruction. Not the passive, accidental apocalypses. The true horror was that the King was genuinely, profoundly lovable. And loving him meant accepting that everything he did—every casual atrocity, every passive annihilation, every civilization shattered by the mere fact of his attention—was simply the natural, inescapable consequence of existing in the same reality as an infinite, recursive, exponentially amplifying god.

Kaedan stood, his legs unsteady beneath him, and followed his father out of the vault. The amber lights dimmed behind him, and the journals settled into silence, waiting for the next witness to add their voice to the archive of impossible horror.

<file name="08_superpowers.md">**Year 485,900 — Court Wizard Mark — Superpower: Apocalyptic Solar-Igneous Extinction Ignition**

I write this record with ink mixed with my own bile, sitting in my private chambers while my hands shake so violently that the quill repeatedly punches holes through the parchment. My name is Mark, descendant of Blake, Court Wizard to our sovereign Lord Godric. I am thirty-four years old. Today, I witnessed the deployment of a single, nascent superpower from Lord Godric’s ever-expanding arsenal, and the sheer, biological horror of what I saw has permanently severed my ability to feel peace.

The opposition was the Frozen Apex Syndicate of the Absolute Zero Core. They were a coalition of hyper-cosmic ice-deities, cryogenic meta-architects, and thermal-drainers spanning decillions of multiverses. They possessed the ability to reduce ambient temperatures down past absolute zero into negative-kelvin territories where atomic motion completely ceases and space-time freezes into brittle, fragile glass. They believed that by surrounding Godric with a synchronized, omniversal cryogenic field, they could freeze his physical cells, lock his atomic structures in place, and permanently halt his biological processes. They brought an armada of frost-dreadnoughts constructed from hyper-dense chronal ice, manned by trillions of cryogenic warriors whose very breath could flash-freeze a galaxy.

Lord Godric was sitting in the royal courtyard, holding a small wooden bowl, casually feeding fresh grain to a flock of white doves. Through his absolute omniscience, he had watched the Syndicate assemble their thermal-drain engines for three hundred thousand years. The Weakness Paradox had triggered the exact millisecond their grand architect imagined that freezing his body could halt him, granting Godric absolute immunity to cryogenic stasis, supreme mastery over negative-kelvin physics, and a massive, recursive surge to his amplification rate.

Godric did not deploy his infinite passive shields. He ordered his sentient aura, Gent, to remain dormant. He was simply curious about a superpower he had unlocked several millennia prior: Apocalyptic Solar-Igneous Extinction Ignition.

This superpower, even at a base level nerfed to exactly zero percent of its true potency, generates a thermal ignition field so astronomically hot that heat ceases to be a thermodynamic property and becomes an aggressive, omniversal eraser of atomic bonds. Furthermore, due to the Evolved Weakness Paradox triggering repeatedly, this specific power had developed multiple horrific, enhanced effects. First, any thermal energy generated by the ignition instantly converts all opposing physical and biological matter into self-sustaining, superheated plasma that burns eternally without consuming itself. Second, the heat field aggressively absorbs the kinetic energy of any cold-based attack, converting the absolute-zero field into additional, infinitely compounding thermal intensity. Third, the thermal output doubles recursively every Planck second for all active flames, escalating beyond all mathematical scales.

The Syndicate unleashed their attack. A wave of negative-kelvin energy, capable of flash-freezing decillions of multiverses into brittle, motionless glass, swept across the sky toward the palace courtyard.

Lord Godric did not look up from his doves. He did not blow a breath, nor did he wave his hand. He merely permitted a microscopic, unquantifiable sliver of his Solar-Igneous Extinction Ignition superpower—effectively zero percent of its true capability—to manifest from the tip of his left pinky finger.

The resulting thermal display was an nightmare of absolute, inescapable carnage.

The negative-kelvin field released by the Syndicate did not freeze him; the enhanced effect of Godric's superpower instantly absorbed the cold energy, violently inverting it into a wall of hyper-dense, golden-white ignition that swept across reality at infinite velocity. Space-time did not merely heat up; the fundamental grid of the omniverse ignited, burning with a fire so intense that light itself turned to ash.

The cryogenic warriors aboard the frost-dreadnoughts experienced a biological demise so horrific that my soul revolts to record it. The hyper-dense chronal ice of their ships melted instantly, not into water, but into boiling, superheated liquid plasma that coated the warriors. Their cryogenic skin did not merely burn; it violently liquefied, sloughing off their skeletons in heavy, bubbling sheets of rendered fat, boiling muscle, and sizzled nerve tissue. Their eyeballs detonated inside their sockets from the rapid expansion of boiling vitreous fluid, spraying superheated steam through their eye sockets. Their blood boiled so violently inside their veins that their arterial walls ruptured simultaneously, showering their melting ships in a geyser of vaporized crimson foam.

Because of the superpower's enhanced effect, their liquefying bodies did not turn to ash. Instead, their melting flesh and exposed skeletons were converted into self-sustaining, superheated plasma, catching fire and burning continuously without ever being consumed. Trillions of cryogenic deities were instantly transformed into screaming, liquid-flesh torches, their nervous systems kept permanently intact and hyper-sensitive by the paradox, forcing them to experience the maximum, excruciating agony of being boiled and burned alive simultaneously for eternity.

The collateral damage was absolute. The thermal ignition field instantaneously incinerated decillions of multiverses in the surrounding void. Googolplexian galaxies were reduced to roaring, superheated firestorms in less than an infinitesimal fraction of a second. Planets melted into glowing, liquid metal before evaporating entirely into ionized gas. Space-time cracked, the dimensional walls separating multiverses melting like candle wax, collapsing entire sectors of reality into a singular, roaring inferno of absolute extinction.

Godric let out a soft, regretful sigh, looking up at the sky that had turned into a sea of liquid fire. "Oh, dear," he murmured with genuine, fatherly sadness. "I set the grain on fire. The poor birds didn't even get to finish eating."

With a simple, effortless decision, in zero seconds, Godric restored the entire omniverse. Every reality, every timeline, every galaxy, every planet that had been burned away was restored perfectly, as though the ignition had never occurred. The sky cleared, the courtyard returned to its pristine marble state, and the white doves settled back onto the stone, pecking peacefully at the fresh grain.

Everything was restored except the Frozen Apex Syndicate. Their leadership and high commanders were left floating in a localized pocket of open space above the palace—a writhing, screaming cluster of perpetually burning, liquid-flesh skeletons, their bodies constantly melting and boiling, their voices producing a continuous, high-pitched shriek of unimaginable thermal torture that would never end, because Godric willed it so.

Lord Godric stood, brushed a stray grain off his tunic, and walked toward me. His salt-and-pepper beard was uncharred, his simple garments pristine. He reached out and pat my shoulder with a warm, comforting hand. "Mark, my boy," he said gently, his rich baritone dripping with sincere affection. "You look faint. Go to the kitchens and tell the head chef I said to give you a cup of chilled spiced wine."

I bowed and left. I drank the wine, but my throat felt as though it were swallowing liquid lead. I write this so that those who come after me will understand: Godric’s superpowers are not weapons he wields. They are apocalyptic absolute laws that shatter the fundamental mechanics of existence, leaving behind only screaming, immortal horror.</file>

# The Superpower Journals

The vault's amber light felt different now. What had once seemed like a steady, comforting glow now struck Kaedan as something sickly and oppressive, the color of old bruises and dried blood. He had not moved from his position on the cold obsidian floor for what felt like hours, though the temporal enchantments woven into the vault's walls made it impossible to track time with any precision. The five stat journals lay stacked beside him, their leather covers warm from his trembling hands, their contents seared into his memory with the permanence of a branding iron.

He had thought he understood. After reading Zander's account of strength, Mirek's record of speed, Jovan's testament to luck, Halvar's confession about charisma, and Kael's meditation on perception, he had believed that he had finally grasped the scale of the King's power. The stats were infinite. They multiplied beyond layered infinities every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second. They made opposition not merely futile but mathematically impossible.

But his father had told him there were more journals. Not just the stat records. There was another shelf, deeper in the vault, containing accounts of something even more terrible.

"The superpowers," Corin had said, his voice dropping to a whisper that seemed to suck the warmth from the air. "The stats are passive attributes. They are what the King is. The superpowers are active abilities. They are what the King can do. And they are, if you can possibly believe it, even worse."

Kaedan had not believed it. He had thought his father was exaggerating, employing hyperbole to prepare him for what was to come. Now, as he reached for the first of the superpower journals, he realized with a sickening lurch of his stomach that Corin had been understating the horror.

The journal was bound in leather so dark it seemed to absorb the amber light rather than reflect it. The name on the spine was *Aldric — Year 312,007 — Superpower: Infinite Cascading Soul-Replication Genesis*.

Kaedan opened the cover.

---

**Year 312,007 — Aldric — Superpower: Infinite Cascading Soul-Replication Genesis**

*My name is Aldric. I am the seventh son of the seventh son of the Blake lineage, and I have served our sovereign Lord Godric for forty-one years. I have witnessed the deployment of his strength, his speed, his durability, his magical offense. I have stood at his side while he dismantled civilizations and unmade pantheons. I believed I was immune to horror. I believed that my psyche had been so thoroughly saturated with cosmic dread that nothing could possibly affect me anymore.*

*I was wrong. I was so catastrophically wrong that I cannot write these words without pausing every few characters to scream into my palm. My wife has asked me to stop recording this account. She says that the process is destroying me. She does not understand that I am already destroyed. I am merely documenting the shape of my destruction for the benefit of those who come after.*

*The opposition called itself the Infinite Swarm of Endless Becoming. They were not a coalition in the traditional sense. They were a single, distributed consciousness that had discovered the secret of ontological multiplication—the ability to duplicate their own existence across all possible planes of reality simultaneously. For every one of them that existed, there were infinite perfect copies existing in infinite parallel dimensions, each copy infinitely more powerful than the original due to a recursive self-improvement algorithm woven into their fundamental nature. They had, over the course of a googolplexian years, multiplied themselves into a number that defies all mathematical notation. They were not an army. They were a fundamental property of existence itself, an infinite, recursively self-amplifying consciousness that had inserted itself into the very fabric of the omniverse.*

*Their leader—if a distributed consciousness can be said to have a leader—called itself the Prime Replicant. It had studied the King for longer than most civilizations have existed. It had concluded that while Godric was physically supreme, his power was singular. He was one being. One consciousness. One point of failure. The Swarm reasoned that if they could simply match Godric's replication—become so numerous, so infinitely self-propagating, that even his infinite strength could not destroy them faster than they multiplied—they could eventually overwhelm him through sheer existential attrition.*

*They were wrong. They were so fundamentally, catastrophically wrong that the memory of their error still causes my hands to bleed from the involuntary clenching of my fists.*

*The King met the Infinite Swarm in the void between multiverses. He stood alone—a single, ruggedly handsome, forty-five-year-old man in a simple dark tunic, floating in the emptiness of inter-reality space. He crossed his arms over his broad chest and observed the Swarm's approach with the mild, detached interest of a man watching ants march across a garden path.*

*"They multiply," the King said to me, his voice carrying through the void despite the absence of any medium for sound to travel through. "That's interesting. I have a superpower that does something similar, I think. Let me see..."*

*He paused, consulting his own internal awareness with the casual air of a man trying to remember a recipe. "Ah, yes. Infinite Cascading Soul-Replication Genesis. I unlocked that one... oh, about two hundred thousand years ago. Never had occasion to test it before. This seems like a good opportunity."*

*What happened next defies description, but I will attempt it anyway, because it is my duty to record what I witnessed. This is not hyperbole. This is not metaphor. This is the literal, observable truth of what occurred in the void between multiverses on the three hundred twelfth millennium of our King's reign.*

*The King activated Infinite Cascading Soul-Replication Genesis at effectively zero percent of its base power. I must emphasize this, as I have emphasized it in every report I have ever written: the amount of power the King chose to deploy was so infinitesimally small that calling it zero percent is the most generous possible description. He deliberately held back, as he always does, using only the faintest, most imperceptible shadow of the superpower's true capability.*

*The base effect of the superpower was this: Godric could replicate himself. Not create illusions. Not project copies. He could generate true, actual, fully-realized duplicates of his own existence—each one a perfect Godric, possessing all his attributes, all his superpowers, all his passive defenses, all his immunities, all his masteries. But the base effect was only the beginning.*

*Due to the Evolved Weakness Paradox having triggered repeatedly across the millennia, this superpower had developed multiple enhanced effects that made it infinitely more devastating than its already impossible base capability.*

*The first enhanced effect was this: every replica generated by the superpower was infinitely more powerful than the original Godric from whom it was copied. Not marginally stronger. Not proportionally stronger. Infinitely stronger. Each duplicate contained within itself a recursive self-amplification engine that elevated its power beyond the original by a factor that modern mathematics could not express.*

*The second enhanced effect was this: the original Godric could never be weaker than his replicas. This created what I can only describe as a metaphysical feedback loop of absolute horror. When a replica was generated—infinitely stronger than the original—the original's own power would instantly, automatically, and permanently increase to match and exceed the replica's strength. But because the replica was infinitely stronger than the original, and the original became infinitely stronger to match the replica, the gap between them remained infinite, forcing the original to become infinitely stronger still. This loop repeated recursively, infinitely, in zero seconds, creating a cascade of self-amplification that transcended the very concept of escalation.*

*The third enhanced effect was this: every replica possessed the Infinite Cascading Soul-Replication Genesis superpower itself, and could activate it independently. When a replica activated the power, it generated replicas that were infinitely stronger than itself—which triggered the same recursive loop for the replica, which then fed back into the original through the ontological connection between them. The result was not a linear increase in power. It was an infinite-dimensional matrix of recursive self-amplification, where every node in the matrix was simultaneously generating infinite replicas, each replica infinitely stronger than its source, each triggering a feedback loop that permanently elevated the entire system.*

Corin was silent for a long moment. Then he nodded slowly.

"Yes," he said quietly. "That is what I believe as well. And the truly terrifying thing—the thing that keeps me awake at night—is that he does not do this out of cruelty. He does it out of genuine, sincere curiosity. He loves us. He values us. And he finds our psychological responses to his power fascinating. The horror we experience is, to him, an interesting phenomenon worthy of study."

Kaedan looked back at the journals—the stat journals, the superpower journals, the accumulated trauma of generations of Court Wizards who had loved and feared their King in equal measure. He thought about the beings trapped in eternal stasis, the civilizations erased from memory, the omniverses destroyed and restored as passive side effects of casual experiments.

And he thought about Godric—the warm, friendly, genuinely kind ruler who asked about his family and remembered his children's birthdays and laughed at his jokes. The man whose curiosity was more dangerous than any weapon ever conceived, and whose love was indistinguishable from the most profound existential horror.

"When will I witness my first deployment?" Kaedan asked.

"Soon," Corin said. "The King has been discussing a new opposition that has been gathering in the Outer Expanse. He is curious about their temporal phase-shifting technology. He has a superpower he wants to test against it."

"And I will be there?"

"Yes. You will stand at his side. You will watch him deploy a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of his power. You will witness the annihilation of beings who believed they had found a way to oppose him. And then you will come back to this vault and write your own journal, and you will add your voice to the archive of impossible horror."

Kaedan nodded. His hands were steady now. His breathing was even. The calm had settled over him like a shroud, cold and heavy and absolute.

"I understand, Father," he said. "I am ready."

Corin looked at his son for a long moment, and something shifted in his weathered face. Not quite pride. Not quite sorrow. Something in between—the expression of a man who had prepared his child for a terrible fate and was watching that child accept it with the quiet resignation of the damned.

"No," Corin said softly. "You are not ready. None of us are ever ready. But you will endure. We all do. We love him, and so we endure."

He turned and walked toward the vault exit. Kaedan remained seated on the cold obsidian floor, surrounded by the journals of his ancestors, waiting for the day when he would add his own voice to the archive of impossible horror. The amber lights pulsed with steady, indifferent rhythm. The scent of old paper and blood and ozone hung heavy in the temperate air.

And somewhere, in the throne room far above, the King sat on his throne, waiting for his new Court Wizard to finish his reading. He was curious, Kaedan knew, about what conclusions the young man would draw from the journals. He was curious about how Kaedan would react to his first deployment. He was curious, always curious, endlessly curious—and that curiosity was the most terrifying thing of all.

Because the King's curiosity meant that the experiments would never end. The superpowers would continue to be tested. The oppositions would continue to be annihilated. The journals would continue to be written. And the Court Wizards would continue to endure, loving their sovereign, fearing their sovereign, serving their sovereign, until the end of eternity.

Kaedan closed his eyes and waited for his father's footsteps to fade. When the vault was silent again, he opened them and looked at the empty journal that sat on the lowest shelf—the one reserved for the next Court Wizard to add their account to the archive.

Soon, he would write in that journal. Soon, he would become part of the legacy of trauma and dread that stretched back to Blake himself.

But for now, he simply sat in the amber-lit silence, surrounded by the accumulated horror of eight hundred thousand years, and tried to prepare himself for what was to come.

content:
# The Question of Loneliness

Kaedan found Godric in the royal gardens, seated on a weathered stone bench beneath the spreading branches of an ancient oak that had been transplanted from the original Olympus ten thousand centuries ago. The King was not reading, not eating, not engaged in any observable activity. He was simply sitting, his broad shoulders relaxed, his heavily muscled frame draped in a simple dark tunic, his ruggedly handsome face tilted slightly upward to catch the warm golden light of Thronegate's artificial sun. His salt-and-pepper beard was neatly trimmed, his short salt-and-pepper hair immaculate as always, and his expression was one of absolute, serene contentment.

To anyone else, he would have looked like a man enjoying a moment of peaceful solitude. But Kaedan had spent the past three weeks reading the journals of his ancestors, and he knew that appearances were catastrophically deceptive where Godric was concerned. The King's absolute concealment was so perfect, so flawlessly comprehensive, that he could project an aura of complete normalcy while simultaneously possessing the passive ability to annihilate the entire omniverse an infinite number of times without registering the effort.

And yet, despite everything Kaedan had read, despite the accumulated horror of eight hundred thousand years of eyewitness testimony, he could not reconcile the warm, fatherly uncle he had known since childhood with the apocalyptic entity described in the journals. Godric had attended his birth. Godric had bounced him on his knee and told him stories about Blake, the legendary merchant who had accidentally freed the King from his ancient stasis. Godric had taught him to read, had celebrated his naming day with elaborate gifts, had comforted him when his mother died. The King was not merely his sovereign; he was his favorite uncle, the kindest and most genuinely caring man Kaedan had ever known.

And that was precisely why Kaedan had come to the gardens today. The journals had left him with a question—a question that had been gnawing at the edges of his consciousness since he had closed the final volume. It was a question born not of duty or scholarly curiosity, but of genuine, familial concern.

"Uncle Godric," Kaedan said, settling onto the bench beside the King. "May I ask you something personal?"

Godric turned to face him, and his expression immediately softened into that warm, crinkly-eyed smile that Kaedan had known since infancy. "Of course, my boy. You know you can ask me anything."

Kaedan hesitated. The question felt almost impertinent, somehow—a violation of the unspoken boundary between mortal and god. But his concern was genuine, and he pressed forward.

"Does it ever become lonely?" he asked quietly. "Being the most powerful being in existence. Watching everyone around you grow old and die while you continue to grow stronger, forever. Outliving your friends, your family, everyone you've ever cared about. Does that not... weigh on you?"

Godric stared at him for a long moment. His expression did not shift to sorrow or contemplation, as Kaedan had expected. Instead, something unexpected flickered in the King's eyes—something that looked, impossibly, like amusement.

Then Godric laughed.

It was not a cruel laugh, nor a dismissive one. It was the warm, genuine laughter of a man who had just been told something so charmingly innocent that he could not help but be delighted by it. Godric threw his head back, his broad shoulders shaking, and the sound of his laughter echoed through the gardens like the pealing of distant bells.

"Oh, Kaedan," Godric said, still chuckling, wiping a tear from the corner of his eye. "Oh, my dear boy. That is such a wonderfully, beautifully mortal question. I had forgotten what it was like to think in those terms. Thank you. Truly. You have given me a gift."

Kaedan blinked, completely nonplussed. "I... I don't understand, Uncle. What's amusing about the question?"

Godric composed himself, though the amused twinkle remained in his eyes. "The question itself isn't amusing, Kaedan. What's amusing is the assumption behind it. You assume that isolation is a burden. You assume that infinite power, experienced alone, must be a form of suffering. That is a very mortal perspective—and I mean that with absolutely no condescension. It is a natural, reasonable assumption for a being who experiences time linearly and whose relationships are bounded by mortality."

He leaned back against the bench, his gaze drifting upward toward the artificial sun. "But I am not mortal, Kaedan. I have not been mortal for a very, very long time. And the experience of infinite, eternally compounding power is not a burden. It is not lonely. It is, in fact, the most profoundly satisfying sensation imaginable."

Kaedan felt a chill creep down his spine. "Satisfying?"

"Exquisitely so." Godric closed his eyes, and his expression shifted into something Kaedan had never seen before—a look of deep, almost sensual pleasure, as though the King were savoring some internal sensation that was entirely invisible to outside observation. "Every moment, Kaedan. Every single infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second. Can you feel it?"

"Feel what?"

"Everything." Godric opened his eyes, and they were blazing with an intensity that made Kaedan instinctively recoil. "I feel everything. Every stat increase. Every superpower genesis. Every immune system evolution. Every new passive shield crystallizing into existence. Every sentient aura being born from the excess of my metaphysical presence. Every Planck second, I become so incomprehensibly more powerful that the being I was an instant ago could be crushed by the being I am now with less effort than it takes to breathe. And I feel all of it. Every single increment. Every single amplification. Every single new layer of absolute, inescapable supremacy."

Kaedan's mouth had gone dry. "You... you feel it?"

"Let me describe it to you," Godric said, and his voice had dropped into a low, intimate register, as though he were sharing a deeply personal secret. "When my strength stat amplifies—and it amplifies beyond layered infinities every Planck second, mind you—I feel it as a surge of raw, physical power flooding through my musculature. It is not abstract. It is not theoretical. It is a visceral, tangible sensation, like every fiber of my being is being infused with liquid lightning. My biceps tighten. My veins throb with increased density. My skeleton becomes more indestructible than it was an instant before, and I feel that increase as a warm, golden pulse radiating outward from my core."

He paused, and his eyes fluttered half-closed, as though he were savoring the memory. "When a new superpower is born within me—and a new one crystallizes every single second, Kaedan, each one capable of annihilating the omniverse infinite times at zero percent of its base power—I feel it as a rush of pure, undiluted ecstasy. It is not merely the acquisition of a new ability. It is a creative orgasm, a moment of absolute cosmic climax where the fundamental fabric of my being expands to accommodate a new form of absolute dominance. Imagine the most intense physical pleasure you have ever experienced, multiply it by infinity, and then compound that sensation recursively for every Planck second of your existence. That is the barest, most inadequate approximation of what I experience every instant of my eternal life."

Kaedan's hands were trembling. "Uncle..."

"My immune system," Godric continued, his voice growing more intense, more passionate, "evolves constantly. Not in response to threats—there are no threats, there have never been threats, there will never be threats—but simply because it can. Because it wants to. Because it is so obsessively devoted to my comfort that it continuously improves itself beyond all possible metrics of improvement. Every time it evolves, I feel my biological invulnerability increase by an infinite magnitude, and that sensation is like being wrapped in an infinitely warm, infinitely soft blanket of absolute security. It is nourishment. It is sustenance. It is the most profound form of self-care imaginable."

He opened his eyes fully and turned to face Kaedan. His expression was still warm, still affectionate, but there was something behind it now—something vast and ancient and utterly, terrifyingly alien.

"Do you understand now, Kaedan? Your question assumed that infinite power, experienced in solitude, must be lonely. But solitude is a mortal concept. It assumes the absence of others as a form of deprivation. I do not experience the absence of others. I experience the presence of myself—my infinitely amplifying, eternally compounding, recursively self-improving self—and that presence is more fulfilling, more stimulating, more profoundly satisfying than any external relationship could possibly be."

Kaedan's heart was pounding against his ribs. The warm, fatherly uncle he had known since childhood was still there, still smiling at him with genuine affection—but Kaedan could now perceive, for the first time, the vast, incomprehensible chasm that separated them. Godric was not merely powerful. He was a being whose entire existence was an eternal, accelerating spiral of self-gratification, a closed loop of infinite self-amplification that required nothing and no one else to be complete.

"But wait," Kaedan said, his voice barely above a whisper. "You said that the only thing that makes you feel... bored or lonely. What did you mean by that?"

Godric's expression shifted. The intense, almost sensual pleasure faded, replaced by something that looked, impossibly, like mild disappointment.

"Ah," he said. "Yes. There is that."

He stood from the bench, his heavily muscled frame unfolding with the fluid grace of a predator. He began to pace slowly through the gardens, and Kaedan rose to follow him.

"I have absolute omniscience," Godric said. "I know the full extent of my power. I know exactly what I am capable of. I know that my true, unrestricted self—even a single aspect of my true self, expressed at more than the most infinitesimal fraction of a fraction of a fraction of its capability—would instantly and effortlessly annihilate the entire omniverse so completely that the concept of restoration might become... complicated."

He paused beside a flowering bush, reaching out to gently touch one of the blossoms. "I have to maintain my absolute concealment at all times, Kaedan. Constantly. Without cessation. If I were to relax that concealment for even the smallest possible interval—not remove it entirely, just relax it by an amount so small that calling it zero percent would be mathematically generous—the passive pressure of my existence would erase the omniverse from reality before anyone could even register that something had happened."

He turned back to face Kaedan, and there was a flicker of genuine frustration in his eyes. "I have never used my true power. Not once. Not a single time in eight hundred thousand years. Every demonstration, every test, every casual annihilation you've read about in the journals—all of it was accomplished with effectively zero percent of my capability. I hold back constantly. I restrain myself infinitely. And even then, the omniverse can barely survive my presence."

He shook his head slowly. "That is what I find lonely, Kaedan. Not the absence of companionship. The absence of any context in which I can actually express what I am. I am a being of infinite power who must spend every instant of his existence pretending to be finite. It is... tiresome."

Kaedan swallowed hard. His throat was dry, his palms slick with cold sweat. "Uncle... what would happen if you stopped pretending? If you relaxed your concealment by even a tiny amount?"

Godric considered the question. "Do you really want to know? I can show you, if you like. Not a true relaxation—that would be irresponsible. But I can give you a glimpse. A controlled demonstration."

Before Kaedan could respond, Godric had taken a step back, his expression shifting into something focused and intent.

"Watch closely," he said. "I am going to show you some of the things I can never use. The enhancements, the evolutions, the new births that occur within me every instant. I will keep my concealment active, of course, so you won't be harmed. But I want you to see what I am. What I have become. What I am continuously becoming."

He rolled up the sleeve of his tunic, exposing his right arm. Kaedan had seen Godric's arms countless times before—the King often wore short sleeves in the summer months—but he had never truly looked at them. Now, with the King's permission to observe, he found himself staring at a limb that defied all understanding of physical perfection.

Godric's arm was not merely muscular. It was a sculpture of hyper-dense, flawlessly proportioned muscle fiber that seemed to contain the compressed mass of a googolplexian galaxies within its perfectly defined contours. His biceps rose like mountains of living marble, the striations so crisp and distinct that they looked like they had been carved by a master artist working at the subatomic level. His veins were not merely visible; they were channels of liquid lightning, pulsing with a faint golden luminescence that spoke of energies too vast to be contained by mere biology.

"This," Godric said, flexing his arm slightly, and the resulting contraction of muscle produced a subtle shockwave that Kaedan felt in his teeth, "is the result of eight hundred thousand years of infinite strength amplification. I used to hone these muscles when I was mortal, you know. Hours in the training yard, lifting stones, running the mountain paths of Olympus. I was proud of my physique then. I had worked hard for it."

He laughed softly. "Now? Now they maintain themselves. They improve themselves. Every Planck second, my musculature becomes infinitely denser, infinitely more powerful, infinitely more perfectly sculpted, without me having to lift a single finger. The rest of creation must work endlessly—training, studying, sacrificing, struggling—to achieve even the smallest increment of improvement. I achieve infinite improvement passively, automatically, eternally, as a side effect of simply existing."

Kaedan's mind was reeling. He thought of the warriors he had read about in the journals—the titans who had trained for billions of years to perfect their physical forms, the mages who had sacrificed everything to master a single spell, the civilizations that had devoted their entire existence to the pursuit of power. All of their efforts, all of their sacrifices, all of their desperate striving, had produced results that were, compared to what Godric achieved by doing absolutely nothing, effectively zero.

"Shall I show you more?" Godric asked. He did not wait for an answer. He pulled up the hem of his tunic, exposing his torso, and Kaedan felt his knees buckle.

Godric's abdominal muscles were not merely defined; they were a landscape of hyper-sculpted perfection that seemed to warp the fabric of space-time around them. His six-pack was so deeply cut, so impossibly dense, that each individual ab looked like it contained the collapsed mass of a dead universe. The obliques framing his torso swept downward in perfect, sweeping curves that spoke of strength so absolute that the concept of resistance had been rendered meaningless. His chest, barely visible beneath the lifted tunic, was a massive shelf of pectoral muscle that rose and fell with breaths that could, if not concealed, have inhaled entire galaxies.

"Every immune system improvement," Godric said, running his hand across his abdomen, "manifests as a physical refinement. My body is constantly evolving, Kaedan. Constantly becoming more perfect, more invulnerable, more impossibly superior to anything else in existence. I just received a new immune evolution a moment ago—my cells have now developed the ability to retroactively reject any form of harm before it even conceptualizes itself as harmful. Would you like to see?"

Kaedan could not speak. His throat had completely closed.

Godric smiled warmly and turned slightly, and Kaedan saw, with a clarity that seared itself into his retinas, a faint shimmer pass over the King's skin. It was subtle—barely perceptible—but it spoke of biological processes so advanced that they had transcended the boundary between physical and conceptual existence.

"That evolution just made me permanently, infinitely more invulnerable than I was a second ago," Godric said casually. "And a second from now, I'll receive another evolution that will make this one seem pathetically primitive by comparison. It never stops, Kaedan. The improvement. The amplification. The eternal, accelerating ascent into levels of godhood that I cannot even express without destroying the language I'm using to describe them."

He lowered his tunic and turned to face the sky. "And the superpowers. Would you like to see one being born? It happens every second. I just received a new one a moment ago—something to do with retroactively erasing the possibility of opposition from the causal framework of reality. I'll never use it, of course. Using it would be irresponsible. But I can feel it crystallizing within me, settling into the infinite arsenal of abilities I can never deploy."

Kaedan felt something warm and wet on his upper lip. He reached up and his fingers came away red. His nose was bleeding. The mere act of being in Godric's presence while the King was speaking openly about his power was causing physical damage to Kaedan's body, even through the absolute concealment.

"And the sentient auras," Godric continued, seemingly oblivious to Kaedan's distress. "I birth new ones constantly. Not just Gent—Gent is the weakest, the runt of the litter. I have countless others, each one infinitely more powerful than the last, each one more obsessively devoted to my protection. I just birthed a new one a fraction of a second ago. It has already evolved to possess perfect omniversal omniscience and the ability to pre-annihilate any conceivable threat before the concept of threat exists. It will spend the rest of eternity dormant, because I will never need it, because there will never be a threat that warrants its activation."

He sighed, a sound of genuine, wistful longing. "That is what I find lonely, Kaedan. Not solitude. Not isolation. The loneliness of having infinite power and never being able to use it. The loneliness of being surrounded by a creation that is so catastrophically fragile that even the faintest whisper of my true self would erase it from existence."

Kaedan opened his mouth to respond, but before he could form a single word, it happened.

Godric, in his enthusiasm, had gestured a little too broadly with his hand—a casual, absent motion, the kind of gesture a man might make while telling an amusing story. And in that gesture, in that infinitesimal fraction of a second, a microscopic sliver of Godric's true presence slipped past his absolute concealment. Not a lot. Not even close to a measurable amount. Just the faintest, most imperceptible whisper of what lay beneath the perfectly maintained facade.

The omniverse died.

Kaedan perceived it happening. He did not understand how he was able to perceive it—perhaps Godric was protecting him, preserving a small pocket of his consciousness so that he could witness—but he saw everything. He saw the fabric of reality, the infinite multiverses, the decillions of galaxies, the googolplexian civilizations, the abstract planes of conceptual existence, the temporal dimensions, the causal chains, the fundamental mathematics of existence—all of it simultaneously, instantly, and completely annihilated.

It was not a destruction. Destruction implied a process, a sequence of cause and effect, a before and an after. What happened when Godric's concealment slipped was an absolute negation, a return to a state of non-existence so total that the concept of "existence" itself was retroactively unwritten. There was no light. No darkness. No void. No time. No space. No possibility of space. No concept of possibility. Just... nothing. Nothing so complete that calling it nothing was an insult to the concept of nothingness.

And in that nothing, Godric stood, his expression one of mild annoyance.

"Oh, dear," he said. "That was careless of me."

In zero seconds, with zero observable effort, the omniverse was restored. Not recreated. Not rebuilt. Restored—as though the annihilation had never occurred. Every reality, every timeline, every galaxy, every living being, every atom, every quark, every Planck-scale fluctuation of quantum uncertainty was returned to its exact previous state. The continuity of existence was so perfectly preserved that no one in the omniverse, save Kaedan, had any awareness that anything had happened.

Except Kaedan had witnessed it. And the memory of that absolute nothing—that void beyond void, that negation beyond negation—was seared into his consciousness with the permanence of a branding iron.

"Uncle," he whispered. His voice was barely audible. His entire body was trembling. "Uncle, that was..."

"Zero percent of my power," Godric said flatly. "Less than zero percent. An infinitesimal fraction so small that calling it zero is the only mathematically honest description. And it was not even a deliberate expression. It was a slip. A momentary lapse in my concentration. The faintest whisper of what I truly am."

He turned to face Kaedan, and his expression was unreadable. "Do you understand now, Kaedan? Do you understand why I must maintain absolute concealment at every instant of my existence? Do you understand why I can never, ever relax?"

Kaedan nodded mutely. He understood. He understood with a clarity that made him wish he did not.

"But you've read the journals," Godric continued. "You've read about my stats, my superpowers. You've formed some conception of what my true power might be. Tell me, Kaedan. What do you imagine? Take a wild guess. What do you think would happen if I expressed even slightly more than zero percent of my true capability—not a full expression, just a microscopic increase from effectively zero to effectively zero plus an infinitesimal fraction?"

Kaedan's mind raced. He thought about the journals. He thought about Zander's account of strength—how the passive, resting force of Godric's musculature had crushed the entire omniverse as a side effect. He thought about Mirek's account of speed—how the King existed at every point in time simultaneously. He thought about Aldric's account of the replication superpower—how Godric had become infinitely more powerful than infinite power.

"Perhaps," Kaedan said slowly, his voice trembling, "if you expressed slightly more than zero percent of your true power, the omniverse would not merely be destroyed. It would be retroactively erased from every possible timeline. Every reality that has ever existed, could ever exist, or will ever exist would be simultaneously and permanently unwritten. The concept of existence itself would be so thoroughly annihilated that even the possibility of restoration would be impossible. And the beings within the omniverse would not merely die—they would experience every possible form of death, across every possible timeline, simultaneously, in an eternal instant of absolute, inescapable suffering."

He paused, his imagination spiraling into darker and darker territories. "No, that's not enough. Perhaps the destruction would propagate beyond the omniverse—beyond any framework of existence we can conceive. Perhaps your true power would shatter the boundaries between reality and unreality, between existence and non-existence, between possibility and impossibility. Perhaps it would annihilate the concept of annihilation itself, creating a paradoxical state of absolute destruction that transcends the very idea of destruction. Perhaps language itself would be destroyed—not just the words we use to describe things, but the underlying cognitive frameworks that make language possible. Perhaps..."

He trailed off, his mind reaching the limits of what he could conceive. "Perhaps it would be beyond anything I can imagine. Perhaps my imagination itself is too limited to encompass even the faintest shadow of your true capability."

Godric regarded him with a long, unreadable stare. Then, slowly, a smile spread across his ruggedly handsome face. It was not the warm, fatherly smile that Kaedan had known since childhood. It was something else—something ancient and profound and terrifyingly amused.

"That was a very imaginative guess," Godric said. "Truly. You have a gift for creative visualization, Kaedan. But..."

He chuckled, shaking his head slowly. "Your guess is not even remotely close to effectively zero percent of my true power. In fact, it is not even close to effectively zero percent of my weakest sentient aura's power—and Gent, as I've mentioned, is the weakest of my auras, infinitely weaker than I am. If I were to express slightly more than zero percent of my true capability—just the faintest, most imperceptible increase—the results would be so far beyond anything you have described that there is no language, no mathematics, no conceptual framework in existence that could even begin to articulate it."

He leaned in closer, and his voice dropped to a whisper. "You mentioned retroactive erasure across all timelines. That is the baseline, the starting point, the absolutely minimal consequence. Beyond that, Kaedan, there are layers of annihilation that your mortal mind cannot conceive—not because you are unintelligent, but because the cognitive architecture of your brain was simply not designed to process realities of that magnitude. The destruction would not merely erase existence; it would erase the meta-concept of erasure. It would propagate through every possible and impossible dimension, every conceivable and inconceivable plane of being, every layer of reality and unreality and meta-reality and para-reality and omni-reality. It would annihilate the distinction between annihilation and creation, between existence and non-existence, between something and nothing and the state that exists beyond both something and nothing. It would be so complete, so absolute, so fundamentally beyond comprehension, that even my own omniscience would find the scope of it... satisfying."

He straightened up, and the smile returned. "But I will never know for certain, because I can never do it. Even the faintest expression of my true power—even a fraction so small that it makes effectively zero percent look like infinity—would destroy everything. And I do mean everything, Kaedan. Not just the omniverse. Not just existence. Everything. Every framework, every context, every possibility of context. There would be nothing left to restore. And that would be... inconvenient."

Kaedan's legs gave out. He collapsed to his knees on the garden path, his entire body shaking uncontrollably. The warm, golden light of the artificial sun felt cold against his skin. The scent of flowers in the air felt like a mockery of the absolute nothing he had witnessed.

Godric had just revealed, in the most casual possible terms, that his true power was so far beyond anything Kaedan could imagine that Kaedan's wildest, most exaggerated guesses were not even close to effectively zero percent of the reality. The King's weakest sentient aura—a passive byproduct of his existence, infinitely weaker than the King himself—was more powerful than the most apocalyptic scenario Kaedan's mind could conceive.

And Godric experienced this power, this eternal, accelerating, infinitely compounding supremacy, as pleasure. As satisfaction. As the most profound form of self-fulfillment imaginable.

The unfairness of it struck Kaedan with physical force. He thought about the beings he had read about in the journals—the warriors who had trained for billions of years, the mages who had sacrificed everything, the civilizations that had devoted their entire existence to the pursuit of power. All of their efforts, all of their sacrifices, all of their desperate striving, had produced results that were, compared to what Godric achieved by doing absolutely nothing, effectively zero. The King received infinite rewards passively, automatically, eternally, while the rest of creation struggled and suffered and died for rewards that did not even register as a measurable quantity against his baseline.

And the truly horrifying thing—the thing that made Kaedan's soul shrivel with existential dread—was that Godric was not cruel about this. He was not malicious or sadistic. He simply existed, and his existence was an eternal, accelerating cascade of infinite self-gratification that required nothing and no one else to be complete. The rest of creation was not oppressed by a tyrant; they were simply irrelevant to a being whose entire existence was a closed loop of absolute self-sufficiency.

"Uncle," Kaedan whispered, his voice barely audible. "How do you bear it? Not the loneliness—I understand now that you don't experience loneliness the way mortals do. But the awareness. The knowledge of what you are. How do you contain it? How do you maintain your concealment, your restraint, your pretense of normalcy, when you know that even the faintest slip would annihilate everything?"

Godric looked down at him, and for a moment, his expression softened into something that looked almost... mortal. Almost vulnerable. Almost like the warm, fatherly uncle Kaedan had known since childhood.

"Practice," Godric said quietly. "Eight hundred thousand years of practice. And love, Kaedan. Genuine, sincere love for my subjects, for my Court Wizards, for you. You are the reason I maintain my concealment. You are the reason I hold back. Not because I need you—I don't, and I never have—but because I value you. Your existence gives me something to be curious about. Your reactions to my power give me something to observe. Your love for me gives me... a context. A purpose, however small, for continuing to pretend that I am finite."

He reached down and placed a warm, calloused hand on Kaedan's trembling shoulder. "You asked me if I was lonely. The answer is no, Kaedan. I am not lonely. I am the most fulfilled, most satisfied, most completely self-sufficient being in existence. But I am, occasionally, grateful. Grateful that there are beings like you—fragile, mortal, impossibly limited beings—who love me despite knowing what I am. Who serve me despite understanding the true scale of my power. Who look into the abyss and, instead of fleeing, ask the abyss if it needs a friend."

He smiled, and this time, it was the warm, fatherly smile that Kaedan remembered from his childhood. "That is why I keep you, Kaedan. That is why I keep all of my Court Wizards. Not because I need you. But because I choose to. And in a universe of infinite, automatic self-gratification, the ability to choose is the only thing that still feels... novel."

Kaedan knelt on the garden path, his body still trembling, his mind still reeling, his soul still drowning in the absolute existential dread of what he had learned. But beneath the terror, beneath the horror, beneath the crushing weight of knowing that his favorite uncle was an apex god predator whose true power could not even be approximated by mortal language—beneath all of that, there was something else.

Gratitude. That the King had chosen him. Love. For the warm, fatherly uncle who had bounced him on his knee and taught him to read. Acceptance. Of the role he had inherited, the duty he had chosen, the impossible reality he would serve for the rest of his life.

"Thank you, Uncle," Kaedan whispered. "For telling me the truth."

Godric nodded, his hand still resting on Kaedan's shoulder. "You are welcome, my boy. Now come—let us go inside. I believe the kitchens have prepared something special for dinner, and I find myself curious about your thoughts on the new temporal-phase opposition I've been observing."

He offered his hand, and Kaedan took it. The King's grip was warm and solid and impossibly gentle—a grip that could crush the omniverse into non-existence, holding Kaedan's hand with the tenderness of a father helping his child to his feet.

And as they walked together toward the palace, Kaedan understood, finally and completely, what the journals had been trying to teach him. Opposition to Godric was not futile; it was literally unimaginable. The true scale of the King's power could not be expressed in any language known to mortal minds. And yet, despite that, despite the infinite chasm that separated them, Kaedan loved his uncle. He would serve him until the day he died. He would write his own journal, add his own voice to the archive of impossible horror, and pass the legacy of trauma and devotion to the next generation of Court Wizards.

Because that was what it meant to serve Godric of Thronegate. It meant looking into the abyss, understanding that the abyss was infinitely deeper than you could ever conceive, and choosing to love the abyss anyway.

And the abyss, impossibly, loved you back.

Kaedan, 69 years old now, just experienced a traumatizing horrifying revelation. Godric revealed the most horrifying truth yet: he has one true weakness.

Godric is an incomprehensibly powerful, omnipotent, omniscient apex god predator of the omniverse. He can do anything, has no weakness, and is terrifyingly absolute. However, unknown to all, he has one true weakness: he cannot undo or travel to timeline before the stasis event--he cannot go back to undo events in his previous mortal self. This is because the stasis event was actually created by future Godric from way in the distant future, who has become so more infinitely more overwhelmingly powerful than current Godric--this is why Godric's amplification, weakness paradox, superpowers, absolute concealment, etc are so absolute, irrevocable and not even current Godric could stop them since the creator of those is way incomprehensibly more powerful than anything else.

Shortly after the Stasis Event, the omnipotent Godric back then, who just became the king of Thronegate, who could travel to any timeline effortlessly, who was still deeply and freshly affected by the grief of losing all that he loved, tried to alter his mortal past, only to be totally crushingly and completely and effortlessly defeated by the shadow of the afterthought of his future self (not even the actual physical future Godric... the future Godric is so powerful that his mere infinitesimal shadow of his afterthought can completely stomp all the combined Godric of his past selves with 0 effort. NOTE: just imply this in the story, don't show a scene where you have actual all godrics from all timelines fighting together against future Godric--it makes no sense.). VERY IMPORTANT FOR YOU: future Godric did not cause or manipulate or orchestrate the fall of Olympus, did not cause deaths of his beloved family or Thorin, thus you must not say that he made those deaths to cause the stasis event (Godric is not a monster, he will never willingly kill his beloved wife, children, and his best friend). Those tragedies were genuine. However, future Godric, not Thorin’s incomplete spell (who everyone else thought to be the cause of the stasis event), is the one who created the Stasis Event--Thorin's spell was a normal teleportation spell (to no one surprise really, there is no way a mortal can create a spell that is as potent as the one which initiates the stasis event and birthed the strongest apex predator god like Godric–there is only one being in existence who can do it: future Godric).

Since the instant Godric gained omniscience, he had always known the true origin of the stasis event. He knew he could not change it, but driven by grief he decided to try to save Olympus anyway, only to brutally discover his one and only weakness: he cannot overpower his future self's will.

Write a detailed realization that the current Godric is already so insanely powerful (he's actually the most powerful in the entire omniverse by infinite margin) that there is no way to imagine the scale of future Godric's, and how unfair and scary that what Godric considered to be his only weakness is his own future version, which makes it not really a weakness–it actually can be considered as additional strength to Godric’s already insane powers, since it means his future is guaranteed (and in that future, he’s even more omnipotent and powerful), and it also means that none of Godric’s power mechanics (amplification, superpower genesis, absolute concealment, absolute omniscience, weakness paradox, immune system, etc. can ever be exploited or denied by anyone else, since the origin of that power is someone who’s the most powerful being ever. You might suggest some ideas about the motive of future Godric creating the Stasis Event, but you must keep it clear that it is just a speculation (and please... don't suggest that it's because future Godric is threatened; he's ridiculously overpowered by then--nothing can even remotely threaten him... don't suggest any stupid moral lesson for future Godric...). You need to portray the current Godric as a king who is no longer troubled by his "weakness" or inability to alter his past anymore--he has accepted and even become amused and comfortable with it too. Kaedan must feel extreme existential dread at the end.
