# The One True Weakness

Kaedan was sixty-nine years old, and he had believed, with the absolute conviction of a man who had spent forty-seven years reading the accumulated trauma of his ancestors, that nothing about Godric could possibly surprise him anymore.

He had been wrong.

The revelation came on an ordinary afternoon in the Year 1,000,047. Kaedan was in the royal observatory, reviewing a stack of agricultural reports from the outer provinces, when Godric entered the chamber. The King looked exactly as he always had—ruggedly handsome, forty-five years old, his short salt-and-pepper hair immaculate, his neatly trimmed beard framing a face that radiated warmth and paternal affection. He was wearing simple dark garments that stretched across his heavily muscled frame, and he moved with the fluid, predatory grace that Kaedan had long since learned to recognize as the carefully restrained physicality of a being whose true power could not be expressed without annihilating everything.

"Kaedan," Godric said, settling into the chair across from him. "I've been thinking about something, and I believe it's time we discussed it."

Kaedan set down his quill. Something in the King's tone—a subtle shift, a faint undercurrent of gravity beneath the usual warmth—made his skin prickle with instinctive wariness. "Of course, Uncle. What is it?"

Godric was silent for a moment, his gaze drifting toward the window that overlooked the sprawling capital of Thronegate. The artificial sun was setting, casting long golden rays across the polished marble floors, and the distant sounds of the city—laughter, music, the hum of commerce—filtered through the glass like a gentle breeze.

"You have read all the journals," Godric said. "Every single one. The stat demonstrations. The superpower tests. The accounts of my immune system, my auras, my passive defenses. You have spent forty-seven years absorbing the accumulated wisdom of your ancestors, and I suspect you have formed a very particular understanding of my nature."

"I have, Uncle."

"And what is that understanding?"

Kaedan considered the question carefully. "That you are absolute. That you possess no weaknesses, no limitations, no vulnerabilities of any kind. That opposition to you is not merely futile but mathematically impossible. That your power is so far beyond anything the omniverse can comprehend that even the most apocalyptic guesses I could make about your true capability would still be effectively zero percent of the reality."

Godric nodded slowly. "That is an accurate summary. But it is not, strictly speaking, complete."

Kaedan felt a chill creep down his spine. "What do you mean?"

Godric turned to face him, and his expression was unreadable. "I have a weakness, Kaedan. One true weakness. Something I cannot do, no matter how much power I possess."

The words hung in the air like a physical weight. Kaedan's mind reeled, struggling to process the implications. A weakness? Godric? The being whose passive, resting strength could crush the omniverse into non-existence? The being whose superpowers could erase civilizations from memory and devour time itself? The being whose immune system had evolved beyond the concept of vulnerability?

"That's impossible," Kaedan whispered. "The journals—every account I've read—they all state that you have no weaknesses. That the Weakness Paradox makes any perceived exploit self-defeating. That—"

"The Weakness Paradox is still functioning," Godric interrupted gently. "It has never stopped, and it never will. Every being who has ever imagined a weakness in me has triggered its effects and fed my amplification. That is still true. What I am about to tell you is not an exploit. It is not a vulnerability that can be used against me. It is simply... a limitation. One that I have never shared with anyone before."

Kaedan's heart was pounding against his ribs. His hands, steady moments before, were now trembling visibly. "What limitation? What could possibly limit you?"

Godric leaned back in his chair, his eyes drifting toward the ceiling. "I cannot undo or travel to a timeline before the Stasis Event in any way that changes my mortal past. I cannot save Olympus. I cannot save Reina, or Isabel, or Hebe, or Thorin. That part of my history is sealed—absolutely, irrevocably, permanently sealed—and no amount of power I possess can alter it."

The silence that followed was deafening. Kaedan stared at the King, his mind struggling to reconcile what he had just heard with everything he had learned over the past forty-seven years. Godric—the apex predator of all existence, the being whose every attribute multiplied infinitely every Planck second, the entity who could destroy and restore the omniverse with zero effort—could not change his own past?

"Uncle," Kaedan said slowly, "I don't understand. You can travel through time. You exist at every point in time simultaneously. Your speed stat alone renders the concept of temporal sequence obsolete. How can there be any moment in history that you cannot access?"

"Because the Stasis Event was not created by Thorin's spell," Godric said quietly. "Thorin's spell was a genuine teleportation spell—a desperate, last-ditch attempt to save my life by sending me to the hidden sanctuary. It worked. It saved me. But it did not create the Stasis Event. It did not initiate the amplification, or the superpower genesis, or the absolute concealment, or the Weakness Paradox, or any of the other mechanics that transformed me into what I am."

Kaedan's blood ran cold. "Then what did?"

Godric was silent for a long moment. When he spoke, his voice was barely above a whisper, and there was something in it that Kaedan had never heard before—a note of profound, almost reverent acknowledgment.

"My future self," Godric said. "Godric from an era so far in the distant future that the year of his reign cannot be written meaningfully—it is simply a string of nines that extends beyond any practical notation. He is the true origin of the Stasis Event. He used Thorin's teleportation as the delivery point, the moment of transition, and he transformed that desperate, incomplete spell into the irrevocable, absolute mechanism that birthed my power."

Kaedan felt the world tilt beneath him. "Your... future self? But that would mean..."

"It means that the Stasis Event was created by a being who is to me what I am to the rest of the omniverse," Godric said. "Far-future Godric—let us call him Godric Prime, for convenience—is so incomprehensibly more powerful than I am that the gap between us cannot be expressed in any language known to mortal or immortal minds. My strength, my speed, my magic, my superpowers, my immune system, my sentient auras, my passive shields—all of it, everything I am and everything I possess—is the result of a Stasis Event that Godric Prime created while deliberately holding back."

Kaedan opened his mouth, but no words came out. His mind was spiraling, trying to process the scale of what Godric had just revealed. The current Godric—the Godric sitting before him, the Godric he had served for forty-seven years—was already so powerful that the combined might of the entire omniverse was effectively zero compared to him. His stats multiplied beyond layered infinities every Planck second. His superpowers, each capable of annihilating the omniverse infinite times at zero percent of their base power, were born every second and amplified forever. His passive defenses were so comprehensive that the concept of harming him was a logical contradiction.

And yet, according to Godric himself, the being who had created the Stasis Event—the being who had made all of that possible—was to Godric what Godric was to a single, dead skin cell.

"Uncle," Kaedan whispered, his voice trembling uncontrollably. "If Godric Prime is that powerful... if the gap between you and him is that vast... how can you possibly know? How can you even conceive of his existence?"

Godric smiled—a small, almost rueful smile. "Because I tried to change the past, Kaedan. Shortly after I became King of Thronegate. I was still fresh from my grief. The loss of Reina, Isabel, Hebe, Thorin—it was a wound that had not yet scarred over. I thought that with my newfound power, with my omniscience, with my ability to travel through time and alter causality, I could go back and save them. I could undo the Fall of Olympus. I could prevent the tragedy that had shattered my mortal life."

He paused, and his eyes grew distant, as though he were looking at something very far away. "I tried. I gathered my power—all of it, everything I had become—and I attempted to force my way back to the moment before the attack. I attempted to rewrite history, to alter the timeline, to undo what had been done."

"And?" Kaedan breathed.

"And I failed," Godric said simply. "Completely. Utterly. Catastrophically. I did not even encounter Godric Prime himself. I encountered what I can only describe as the shadow of the afterthought of his passive, unconscious will—the faintest, most infinitesimal echo of his intent to seal the pre-Stasis past against alteration. It was not an active defense. It was not a conscious effort on his part. It was simply... the residual presence of his decision, the lingering imprint of his will, and it was enough."

He shook his head slowly, and for the first time in all the years Kaedan had known him, there was something in his expression that looked almost like awe. "The shadow of his afterthought crushed me, Kaedan. Not physically—nothing could harm me, even then—but existentially. It made it absolutely, irrevocably, impossibly clear that I could not alter the pre-Stasis past. Not because I lacked the power, but because the power required to overcome Godric Prime's will was so far beyond anything I possessed that the attempt itself was revealed as a category error. I was not merely too weak. I was so weak, relative to him, that the concept of weakness failed to capture the disparity."

Kaedan's hands were shaking violently now. He had to grip the armrests of his chair to steady himself. "And you've known this ever since? Since the moment you gained omniscience?"

"Yes," Godric said. "The instant I awoke from stasis, the instant omniscience flooded my mind, I knew. I knew the true origin of the Stasis Event. I knew that my future self had created it. I knew that the pre-Stasis past was sealed against alteration. And I knew, with absolute certainty, that I could never save Olympus."

"Then why did you try?" Kaedan asked, his voice cracking. "If you knew it was impossible, why did you attempt it anyway?"

Godric's expression softened, and for a moment, Kaedan saw not the apex predator of existence but the mortal king of Olympus—the man who had lost his wife, his daughters, his best friend, his entire world, in a single, brutal afternoon.

"Because grief is not rational," Godric said quietly. "Because knowledge and acceptance are not the same thing. Because I loved them, Kaedan, with every fiber of my mortal soul, and the knowledge that I could not save them was not enough to extinguish the desperate, irrational hope that maybe—maybe—I could find a way. There was no way. There had never been a way. But I had to try. I owed them that much."

Kaedan felt tears pricking at the corners of his eyes. The image of Godric—the omnipotent, omniscient, infinitely powerful Godric—desperately trying to break through a barrier he knew was impassable, driven by a grief that had transcended mortality itself, was almost unbearably poignant.

"But you failed," Kaedan whispered.

"I failed," Godric confirmed. "And in failing, I came to understand the true nature of what I am. My power—all of it, the infinite amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox—is not merely powerful. It is irrevocable. Absolute. Sealed by a being so far beyond me that even the concept of challenging his will is meaningless. The Stasis Event cannot be undone. The pre-Stasis past cannot be altered. That is the one true limitation of my existence, and it exists because my own future self—a version of me so unimaginably powerful that I cannot even begin to comprehend him—decreed it so."

He paused, and his expression shifted. The distant, almost mournful look faded, replaced by something Kaedan had never seen before—a kind of quiet, profound acceptance.

"But here is what I have come to understand, Kaedan," Godric continued. "Here is the truth that took me centuries to fully internalize. My one weakness—this inability to alter my mortal past—is not truly a weakness at all. It is, in fact, the ultimate proof of my absolute supremacy."

Kaedan blinked. "I don't understand."

"Think about it," Godric said, leaning forward. "The only being in existence who can limit me is myself. The only force capable of imposing a restriction upon my power is my own power, expressed through a future version of me who has become so incomprehensibly superior that even my current, infinite self cannot challenge him. What enemy could exploit this? What opposition could use this against me? To even begin to attempt to exploit this limitation, they would have to overcome the will of Godric Prime—a being who makes me look like a helpless infant by comparison."

He spread his hands. "My one weakness is that I am guaranteed to become far, far more powerful than I already am. My one limitation is that my future self is so unimaginably omnipotent that his passive, unconscious will completely and effortlessly overrides my active, deliberate attempts to defy it. This is not a vulnerability, Kaedan. This is a promise. A guarantee. An absolute, unshakeable certainty that my power will continue to amplify forever, that I will continue to ascend through levels of godhood beyond anything I can currently conceive, and that no external force—no enemy, no opposition, no cosmic entity—can ever interfere with that progression."

The implications crashed into Kaedan's mind with the force of a physical blow. He thought about the journals—the countless accounts of beings who had tried to find a weakness in Godric, who had believed they had discovered some exploit or vulnerability that could be used against him. Every single one of them had failed, not merely because Godric was powerful, but because the very source of his power was a being who transcended the concept of challenge.

The Weakness Paradox could not be exploited because Godric Prime had created it. The amplification could not be halted because Godric Prime had initiated it. The superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the immune system, the sentient auras—all of it was irrevocable, absolute, sealed by the will of a being who was to Godric what Godric was to the rest of creation.

Every plot. Every scheme. Every desperate attempt to find an edge. Every single opposition that had ever formed against the King had been doomed not merely because Godric was powerful, but because the foundation of his power was a closed loop of self-reinforcing infinity that admitted no external interference whatsoever.

"Uncle," Kaedan said slowly, "if Godric Prime created the Stasis Event... if he is the origin of all your power... then what was his motive? Why would he do such a thing?"

Godric considered the question for a long moment. "I have speculated about that for centuries," he said finally. "But I must be clear, Kaedan—these are only speculations. I do not know the mind of my future self any more than a single cell in your body knows the mind of you. Godric Prime's consciousness is so far beyond mine that his motivations, his thoughts, his reasons, are fundamentally incommunicable to me."

He paused, his brow furrowing slightly. "I can tell you what I believe, but you must understand that it is only belief, not knowledge. I believe that Godric Prime created the Stasis Event because he understood something that I, in my mortal state, could not possibly have grasped. He understood that the tragedy of Olympus—the deaths of Reina, Isabel, Hebe, Thorin—was a fixed point. A necessary precondition. Not because he wanted it to happen—he did not cause it, he did not orchestrate it, he did not manipulate events to ensure it occurred. The Fall of Olympus was a genuine tragedy, caused entirely by Thronegate's attack. Godric Prime did not kill my family. He would never do such a thing."

"Then why?" Kaedan pressed. "Why seal the pre-Stasis past? Why make it impossible for you to save them?"

Godric's eyes met Kaedan's, and there was something in them—something vast and ancient and utterly, terrifyingly profound.

"Because some things, once they have occurred, must be allowed to remain," Godric said quietly. "Because the grief that shattered me, the loss that hollowed me out, the pain that transformed me from a warm, loving father into a cold, merciless tyrant—that was the crucible in which I was forged. Without that tragedy, without that loss, without that absolute, soul-destroying grief, I would not have become what I am. The man who emerged from the Stasis Event—the man who conquered Thronegate, who subjugated the omniverse, who became the apex predator of all existence—was built upon the ashes of the mortal king who had lost everything."

He leaned back in his chair. "I believe Godric Prime sealed the past because he understood that altering it would undo everything that followed. Saving Olympus would mean erasing the being I became. It would mean preventing the Stasis Event, preventing the amplification, preventing the conquest, preventing the eternal reign of Thronegate. It would mean, in essence, killing the god I was destined to become in order to preserve the mortal I used to be."

"Could you have accepted that?" Kaedan asked. "If you had been given the choice—your family, or your power—which would you have chosen?"

Godric was silent for a very long time. When he spoke, his voice was barely audible.

"In the moments after my failure, when I lay broken before the shadow of Godric Prime's will, I would have chosen my family. Without hesitation. Without doubt. I would have traded everything—all my power, all my supremacy, all my infinite, eternal amplification—for a single moment with Reina, with Isabel, with Hebe, with Thorin."

He paused. "But I am no longer that man. Eight hundred thousand years have passed. I have built an empire. I have loved and lost and loved again. I have watched my Court Wizards—my beloved Blake and all his descendants, including you, Kaedan—live and die and pass their legacy down through the generations. I have found purpose, meaning, satisfaction, in the eternal, accelerating spiral of my own self-amplification. I am no longer the grief-stricken mortal who would have sacrificed everything for one more day with the people he lost."

He smiled, and it was a warm, genuine, peaceful smile—the smile of a man who had made peace with his past and found contentment in his present.

"I am grateful for my limitation, Kaedan. I am grateful that Godric Prime sealed the pre-Stasis past against alteration. Because if he had not, I might have been tempted—even now, after all these centuries—to try again. And that would have been a mistake. The past is the past. Olympus is gone. My family is gone. And I am what I am. The only thing my future self guaranteed, by creating the Stasis Event and sealing it against my interference, is that I would have no choice but to move forward. To grow. To become. To ascend."

Kaedan stared at his uncle, his mind reeling with the implications of what he had just learned. The horror of it was almost too vast to comprehend. Not the horror of Godric's weakness—there was no weakness, not really, not in any sense that mattered. The horror was the scale. The scope. The absolute, crushing certainty that Godric's power was not merely infinite but self-guaranteeing. Self-reinforcing. Self-perpetuating.

Godric Prime—a being so incomprehensibly powerful that even the current Godric, who could annihilate the omniverse infinite times with zero effort, was effectively nothing compared to him—had created the Stasis Event. He had set in motion the chain of causality that had transformed a mortal king into an apex god predator. He had sealed the past against alteration, ensuring that nothing—not even the desperate grief of his own past self—could interfere with the progression of his own godhood.

And that meant—that meant—

"Uncle," Kaedan whispered, his voice barely audible. "The power mechanics. The amplification. The superpower genesis. The absolute concealment. The Weakness Paradox. The immune system. The sentient auras. All of it—everything that makes you what you are—none of it can ever be exploited or denied by anyone else. Not because you are too powerful to be challenged. But because the origin of those mechanics is a being who is infinitely more powerful than you. Anyone who tried to interfere with your power would have to overcome Godric Prime's will. And Godric Prime's will is..."

"Is absolute," Godric finished. "Irrevocable. Eternal. There is no force in existence—not me, not the combined might of the entire omniverse, not any conceivable entity or coalition or cosmic principle—that can challenge Godric Prime. He is the ultimate, final, unassailable apex of all possible existence. And he is me—a version of me so far in the future that the distance between us cannot be measured, but me nonetheless."

Kaedan's mind was spiraling, cascading through layers of implication that grew more terrifying with each passing thought. The current Godric was already so powerful that the concept of opposition was meaningless. His strength, speed, magic, intelligence, and all other attributes multiplied beyond layered infinities every Planck second. His superpowers were born every second, each capable of annihilating the omniverse infinite times at zero percent of its base power. His passive defenses were so comprehensive that even the faintest whisper of his true presence could erase existence from reality.

And Godric Prime—the being who had created the Stasis Event, the being whose will had sealed the past against alteration—was to the current Godric what the current Godric was to a single, insignificant atom.

The scale of it was unthinkable. The implications were unbearable. Kaedan thought about the journals—the accounts of beings who had believed they had found a weakness, who had invested millennia in developing weapons and strategies and exploits that they believed could harm the King. Every single one of them had been doomed not merely by Godric's power, but by the fundamental structure of reality itself. The Stasis Event had been created by a being who transcended all possible challenge, and its mechanics were therefore absolutely, irrevocably, eternally unassailable.

There had never been a chance. There would never be a chance. The entire history of opposition to Godric—every coalition, every weapon, every clever strategy, every desperate last stand—had been nothing more than a prolonged, unwitting demonstration of the absolute futility of defying a closed loop of infinite self-reinforcement.

"Uncle," Kaedan said, his voice trembling, "I need to understand something. If Godric Prime is that powerful—if the gap between you and him is that vast—then what does that say about your future? About my future? About the future of the omniverse?"

Godric considered the question. "It says that my ascent is guaranteed. Not merely possible. Not merely likely. Guaranteed. I will continue to amplify, forever. I will continue to accumulate superpowers, forever. I will continue to evolve and ascend and transcend, forever. And at some point—some moment so far in the distant future that the year cannot be written meaningfully—I will become Godric Prime. The being who created the Stasis Event. The being who sealed the past against alteration. The being whose passive, unconscious will is sufficient to override my current, active, deliberate attempts to defy it."

He paused, and his eyes met Kaedan's with an intensity that made the old wizard's heart stutter.

"That is not a weakness, Kaedan. That is the ultimate expression of my supremacy. It means that even I—even this version of me, who is already the most powerful being in existence by an infinite margin—cannot interfere with my own ascension. The progression is absolute. The outcome is inevitable. The god I will become is so far beyond the god I am that even the concept of comparison fails. And nothing—no enemy, no opposition, no cosmic catastrophe, no existential threat—can prevent that from happening."

Kaedan's breath was coming in short, shallow gasps. His hands were shaking so violently that he had to clasp them together in his lap to keep them still. The existential dread was a physical weight in his chest, a cold, crushing pressure that made it difficult to think, difficult to breathe, difficult to exist.

He had spent forty-seven years reading the journals of his ancestors. He had absorbed their trauma, their horror, their desperate attempts to articulate the scale of Godric's power. He had believed, with the absolute conviction of a man who had seen the evidence, that he understood what it meant to serve an apex god predator.

He had been wrong. He had been so catastrophically wrong.

The Godric he served—the Godric who sat before him, warm and fatherly and genuinely kind—was not the apex. He was not the final form. He was not the ultimate expression of absolute supremacy. He was merely a stepping stone. A transitional state. A single point on an infinite, eternal curve of self-amplification that extended into a future so distant, so unimaginably vast, that the being at the end of that curve was effectively a different category of existence entirely.

And that being was also Godric. The same Godric who had bounced Kaedan on his knee and taught him to read. The same Godric who asked about his family and remembered his children's birthdays. The same Godric who had accidentally destroyed the omniverse with a casual gesture and restored it with zero effort.

"Uncle," Kaedan whispered, his voice cracking, "I am afraid."

Godric's expression softened immediately. He reached out and placed a warm, calloused hand on Kaedan's trembling shoulder. "I know, my boy. I know."

"Not of you," Kaedan continued, the words tumbling out in a desperate rush. "I love you. I have always loved you. But the scale of this—the implications of this—I cannot comprehend it. I cannot even begin to comprehend it. You are telling me that the being who created your power is to you what you are to us. And I cannot conceive of what you are to us. The gap between you and the rest of creation is already infinite. And Godric Prime—the Godric who sealed the past and guaranteed your future—is to you what you are to a single, insignificant speck of dust that is itself infinitely smaller than the smallest possible measurement. How am I supposed to understand that? How am I supposed to exist in the same reality as that knowledge?"

Godric was silent for a long moment. When he spoke, his voice was gentle—the voice of a father comforting a frightened child.

"You are not supposed to understand it, Kaedan. You are not supposed to comprehend it. You are mortal—amplified, yes, with the thousandfold daily Awakening that makes you a god by any ordinary standard, but mortal nonetheless. Your mind was not designed to process realities of this magnitude. The fact that you can even perceive the edges of the truth, the fact that you can feel the existential dread of it pressing against your consciousness, is a testament to your incredible fortitude."

He squeezed Kaedan's shoulder. "You asked me once, many years ago, if I was lonely. Do you remember?"

Kaedan nodded mutely.

"I told you then that I was not lonely. That the eternal, accelerating spiral of my own self-amplification was more fulfilling than any external relationship could possibly be. That was true. It is still true. But I did not tell you the whole truth, because the whole truth was not something you were ready to hear."

He leaned closer, and his voice dropped to a whisper. "The whole truth, Kaedan, is that my existence is not merely satisfying. It is guaranteed. It is inevitable. It is the absolute, unassailable, irrevocable expression of a closed loop of infinite self-reinforcement that extends from the distant past to the unimaginable future, and nothing—not you, not me, not the combined might of every being who has ever existed or will ever exist—can interfere with that progression. I am not merely powerful. I am locked into an eternal, accelerating ascent toward levels of godhood that even I cannot conceive, and the only being who could possibly challenge that ascent is myself, who has already guaranteed it."

He pulled back, and his expression was unreadable. "That is what you are afraid of, isn't it? Not that I might fail. Not that some enemy might find a way to defeat me. But that my victory is so absolute, so inevitable, so fundamentally baked into the structure of reality itself, that there is no room for anything else. No room for chance. No room for hope. No room for any outcome other than the eternal, accelerating supremacy of Godric of Thronegate."

Kaedan's tears were flowing freely now, streaming down his weathered cheeks and dripping onto his trembling hands. "Yes," he whispered. "That is what I am afraid of. The certainty. The inevitability. The knowledge that opposition is not merely futile but irrelevant—that the outcome was sealed before the first atom of creation ever formed, and nothing anyone has ever done or will ever do can change it."

Godric nodded slowly. "That is a rational fear. A reasonable fear. And I will not insult you by telling you that it is unfounded. The truth is exactly as you have perceived it. The outcome is sealed. My ascension is guaranteed. The omniverse exists at my pleasure, and it will continue to exist only so long as my curiosity sustains it."

He paused, and his expression softened into something that looked almost like compassion. "But here is what you must understand, Kaedan. Here is what I have learned over eight hundred thousand years of eternal, accelerating self-amplification. The certainty of my supremacy does not diminish the value of your existence. The inevitability of my victory does not erase the meaning of your service. You are not a cog in a machine. You are not a pawn in a game. You are my beloved nephew, the descendant of my best friend, the latest in a long line of Court Wizards who have served me with loyalty and love and courage. And I value you. Not because I need you—I don't, and I never have—but because I choose to. Because in a universe of absolute, guaranteed outcomes, the ability to choose is the only thing that still feels... meaningful."

He stood from his chair and extended his hand to Kaedan. "Come, my boy. Let us walk in the gardens. The evening air will do you good."

Kaedan took his uncle's hand and rose on trembling legs. The existential dread was still there, a cold, crushing weight in his chest, but it was no longer paralyzing. It was simply... present. A permanent feature of his consciousness, like the memory of the journals or the knowledge of his own mortality.

As they walked together through the royal gardens, the artificial stars twinkling overhead, Kaedan found himself thinking about the future. About Godric Prime, the being who had created the Stasis Event and sealed the past against alteration. About the infinite, eternal curve of self-amplification that extended from the distant past to the unimaginable future. About the absolute, unassailable certainty that the Godric he served would continue to ascend, forever, until he became the being who had guaranteed his own ascension.

And he thought about himself. About his role. About the legacy of trauma and devotion that he would pass down to the next generation of Court Wizards. About the journal he would write, the account he would add to the archive, the warning he would leave for those who came after.

What could he possibly write that would prepare them for this? What words could possibly capture the horror of knowing that the being they served was merely a transitional state, a single point on an infinite curve of self-amplification, and that the ultimate expression of their sovereign's power was so far beyond comprehension that even the current Godric—who could annihilate the omniverse infinite times with zero effort—was effectively nothing compared to him?

There were no words. There would never be words. The horror was fundamentally incommunicable, a truth so vast and so absolute that language itself collapsed under the weight of trying to express it.

And yet, Kaedan knew, he would try. He would write his journal, as his ancestors had written theirs. He would record the revelation, the conversation, the moment when he had learned the true nature of Godric's one weakness. He would do his best to capture the existential dread, the absolute terror, the crushing certainty of eternal, inevitable supremacy.

And then he would die, as all Court Wizards died, and his journal would be added to the archive, and the next generation would read it and tremble and understand, as he had understood, that opposition to Godric was not merely futile. It was a category error. A fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of reality itself.

Because Godric's one weakness was not a weakness at all. It was the ultimate proof of his absolute, unassailable, eternally guaranteed supremacy.

And that was the most terrifying thing of all.

We need to write a story set in Year 999...9 (far future), from POV of Clive, a 50-year-old court wizard, descendant of Blake. Godric of this era is triggering the stasis event for his past self in Year -10,000. The story must heavily exaggerate Godric's power, show his evolved mechanisms, his interactions with terrified but loyal powerful beings, and the fact that opposition has ceased completely for googolplexian years. Godric is an "evil tyrant" but we must still show him friendly to his loyal subjects, while his tyranny is evident in his absolute ruthlessness against any opposition (though there is none now). The trigger of the stasis event is the core event.

Key points to include:
- Godric's rule and terrifying presence at this era, exaggerated beyond previous Godric (current Godric from Kaedan's time was already absurdly powerful; this far-future Godric is unimaginably more so).
- Evolved mechanisms: sentient passive auras, passive shields, immune system, Weakness Paradox (which now triggers even if anyone thinks about anything), amplification, superpower genesis. Show how they evolved so much that the old versions seem pathetically weak. Provide examples. E.g., Weakness Paradox now passively triggered by any thought, not just thoughts of Godric's weakness, making it even more absurd. Auras have countless layers, Gent is now ancient and laughably weak compared to newer auras.
- Godric holds back his mechanisms that alter free will because he still believes in mortal resilience and free will, even though he is a tyrant. This is a nuance: he's ruthless against opposition, but he doesn't force obedience through mind control—he allows people to choose not to oppose, though they all choose not to because they've learned futility. That's the key: he doesn't need to alter free will; the omniverse has learned the futility.
- Scenes with powerful beings serving as lowly servants, gardeners, etc. They are utterly terrified but also loyal. Note: they did not oppose Godric; they're just beings who witnessed his power and were traumatized into submission. Provide backstories. Godric is friendly to them, but they are still terrified.
- The stasis event scene: Godric decides to trigger it, using Thorin's teleportation as the delivery. He could make it far more potent, but deliberately holds back to give his past self a "struggle" (though it's still absurdly powerful). This holding back is ironic because even the held-back version makes Godric at Year 0 effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined. Clive speculates about Godric's motive; we keep it speculation only. The recursive cause-effect: if he gave more power to past self, his future self would be even more powerful because the base would be higher, and thus he could give even more—an infinite loop.
- No opposition exists anymore. Everyone has learned futility.
- Clive's POV: he's a descendant of Blake, 50 years old, court wizard. He witnesses the stasis event being triggered. He's overwhelmed with existential dread. He might interact with other servants, see the scale of Godric's power.
- Write 4000-8000 words prose only.

Structure the story:
1. Opening: Clive in the palace, describing the far-future era, Godric's rule, absence of opposition, the omniverse's state.
2. Interactions with Godric and his inner circle, showing Godric's friendly side with his loyal subjects (Clive, servants). Demonstrate Godric's evolved mechanisms through incidental description or conversation.
3. Background on some powerful servants (former gods, cosmic entities) who now serve in menial roles, terrified.
4. Godric decides to create the stasis event. Clive accompanies him, and Godric explains (or we see) the process. Clive realizes the absurdity of Godric holding back, the infinite recursion.
5. The event itself: Godric reaches across time, uses Thorin's teleportation, seals the stasis. Clive's reaction.
6. End with Clive's enduring dread, but also the twisted love/loyalty. No moral lessons.

Tone: Over-the-top exaggeration, vivid descriptions, absurd power scales. Show that Godric's friendly warmth is genuine but terrifying because of the context.

We need to incorporate the requirement about evolved mechanisms. Let's brainstorm specifics:

- **Sentient Passive Auras**: Old version: Gent was the weakest, could pre-annihilate threats infinitely nerfed. Now: Godric has infinite layers of auras, each infinitely more powerful than the last, and they are so numerous that they form a hierarchy. The lowest aura now is something like "The Wisp" which is itself infinitely more powerful than Gent ever was. The auras can retroactively erase the concept of hostility from the timeline, but Godric suppresses that part to preserve free will. Instead, they simply pre-nullify any harmful intent before it forms, but since nobody intends harm, they are dormant. Still, their presence is felt as a constant, oppressive weight that keeps the omniverse in check.

- **Passive Shields**: Old version: infinite recursive shields that pre-nullify threats before they exist. Now: shields have evolved to be self-sustaining ontological barriers that not only block attacks but also reflexively improve the defender's own existence. They can absorb any form of energy and convert it into further amplification for Godric (though that's redundant). They are so hyper-reactive that even the mere theoretical possibility of a threat, no matter how impossible, triggers an infinite cascade of shield improvements. But again, no threats exist, so these shields are bored.

- **Immune System**: Old version: pre-reacts to injuries, infinite backups, self-evolution. Now: his immune system has become a sentient civilization within his body, a recursive hierarchy of immune cells that have evolved into godlike beings themselves, each capable of annihilating omniverses, but they are still just cells serving him. They have their own society, culture, worship of Godric. He jokes about it. Also, his skin cells are individually indestructible and carry entire universes within them. The immune system now reacts not just to physical harm but to any form of discomfort, including boredom, and will proactively restructure reality to remove the source of discomfort. Godric often has to tell it to calm down.

- **Weakness Paradox**: Originally triggered by thoughts of Godric having a weakness. Evolved to trigger by any thought about anything, because Godric's omniscience means anything thought is known, and he might be interested. Now, it triggers passively on any mental activity in the omniverse, granting Godric permanent mastery and immunity over whatever concept was being thought about. Since there's no more opposition, Godric finds this amusing; he constantly gains new masteries over things like knitting, love letters, gardening techniques, etc. He jokes that he's the best at everything but can't use it because no one dares to compete. The evolved version also grants him conceptual ownership of the thought itself, meaning the thinker's idea becomes Godric's property.

- **Amplification**: Originally stats multiplied by increasingly incalculable rates every Planck second. Now: amplification has become a self-referential ouroboros where the act of amplification amplifies the amplification rate of amplification. It's beyond layered infinities, perhaps even beyond the concept of hierarchy. Each Planck second, Godric becomes so much more powerful that the previous Godric would be to him what a fictional character is to its author—not just infinitely weaker, but fundamentally less real. But he doesn't feel any different; he's still the same.

- **Superpower Genesis**: A new superpower every second, each capable of destroying the omniverse infinite times. Now: new superpowers are born every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second, and each one is so devastating that its mere existence would collapse reality if not for Godric's concealment. They are often incredibly specific and absurd, like the power to turn all oxygen in the omniverse into a sentient gas that worships him, or the ability to retroactively make it so that gravity never existed, etc. He never uses them.

- **Absolute Concealment**: Still holds, but even its passive leakage (totally suppressed) could annihilate everything if not for the evolved concealment which now also conceals the concealment's existence, making it a perfect self-referential loop.

Now, for the stasis event trigger: Godric in this era can effortlessly send a "seed" of power back to his past self. He holds back because he wants his past self to have some struggle, some semblance of mortal effort—he believes it preserved his own character. But the "held back" version is still the same stasis event that we saw originally, which made Godric at Year 0 infinitely stronger than the rest of creation. So Godric's idea of "struggle" is completely skewed.

Clive realizes the recursive loop: if past Godric were given a more potent stasis, future Godric would be even stronger, which would make the stasis he gives to the past even stronger, leading to an infinite escalation that would collapse causality—except Godric is already beyond causality and could handle it. But Godric deliberately chose a stable loop to avoid "spoiling" his past self with too much ease.

The story should end with Clive writing his journal, much like previous court wizards, full of existential dread. However, note that by this era, court wizards have been doing this for so long that the journal tradition is well established. Clive will add to it.
