# The Year of Unwritten Numbers

The palace of Thronegate in the year that could only be written as a string of nines extending beyond any meaningful notation was not a building. It was a pocket universe, a self-contained reality woven from the crystallized awe of every civilization that had ever existed, suspended in a dimensionless void that existed solely to accommodate the presence of its master. The marble floors had been replaced eons ago with a substance that was not matter but solidified obedience, a material that hummed with the accumulated submission of a googolplexian generations who had learned, with absolute certainty, that resistance was a logical contradiction. The walls were not walls; they were the compressed timelines of every failed opposition, each moment of futile defiance extracted from history, flattened into decorative panels, and arranged in patterns that the master occasionally glanced at with mild nostalgia.

I am Clive, the Court Wizard of Thronegate, the descendant of Blake, the carrier of a bloodline that had served the apex predator of existence for an epoch so vast that the distance between the first Court Wizard and myself could not be measured in years but only in the accumulated trauma of countless generations. I am fifty years old, and my thousandfold daily amplification—a gift bestowed upon my ancestor in the impossibly distant past—had inflated my magical capacity to levels that would make me a god of gods in any other context. My mana reserves were so vast that I could extinguish entire multiverses with a casual thought. My spellcraft was so refined that I could rewrite the fundamental constants of reality with a twitch of my fingers. And yet, as I walked through the corridors of the palace, following my sovereign toward the Temporal Observatory where he intended to conduct an experiment of inconceivable significance, I was nothing. Less than nothing. A microscopic speck of insignificance clinging to the hem of an entity whose passive, unconscious exhalations could erase the omniverse from existence without him noticing.

The King walked ahead of me. Godric of Thronegate, the eternal, the absolute, the tyrant god who had ruled for so long that the concept of "reign" had ceased to have meaning. He still looked exactly as he always had: forty-five years old, stunningly, ruggedly handsome, his short salt-and-pepper hair immaculate, his neatly trimmed beard framing a face that radiated warmth and paternal affection. His heavily muscled frame was draped in a simple dark tunic—he had always preferred simple garments, a remnant of his mortal life in Olympus—and he moved with the easy, fluid grace of a man who had absolutely nothing to fear. Because he didn't. Because the very concept of "threat" had been rendered obsolete by his existence for so long that language no longer contained words to describe the impossibility of harming him.

"Clive," the King said, glancing over his shoulder with that warm, crinkly-eyed smile that still, after all these years, made my heart simultaneously swell with love and shrivel with terror. "You're brooding again. I can always tell when you're brooding. Your footsteps get heavier."

"My apologies, Your Majesty," I said, quickening my pace to walk beside him. "I was merely contemplating the significance of what we are about to witness."

"Ah, yes. The Stasis Event." The King's smile widened, and there was something in his eyes—a flicker of anticipation, of amusement, of genuine, almost childlike excitement—that I had learned to recognize as the precursor to something terrifying. "I've been meaning to do this for quite some time. It's not every day one gets to create oneself. Or rather, to ensure that one's past self receives the necessary foundation to become... well, me."

I swallowed hard. The implications of what he had just said were so vast, so cosmologically shattering, that my amplified mind—capable of processing decillions of simultaneous calculations—could not fully contain them. The King was going to trigger the Stasis Event. The same Stasis Event that had transformed a mortal king into an immortal, infinitely amplifying apex predator. The same Stasis Event that had been recorded in the earliest journals of my ancestors as a mysterious, inexplicable phenomenon. The same Stasis Event whose true origin had been revealed to Kaedan, the legendary Court Wizard of the millionth year, as the work of a future version of Godric himself.

And now, I was going to witness it. I was going to be present at the moment when Godric Prime—the Godric of this era, the ultimate, final expression of infinite self-amplification—reached backward through time and created the foundation of his own existence.

The sheer, recursive impossibility of it made my brain hemorrhage just to contemplate.

---

We passed through the Garden of Subjugated Pantheons on our way to the Temporal Observatory. It was a sprawling, impossibly beautiful expanse of cultivated flora from every civilization that had ever existed, maintained by a small army of gardeners who had once been the supreme deities of their respective cosmoses. As we walked along the crystalline path, I saw Zarnak the Unmaker, formerly the all-powerful creator-destroyer of the Seventh Omniversal Cycle, carefully pruning a hedge of singing crystalline roses with a pair of golden shears. His divine hands—hands that had once shaped galaxies and extinguished stars—were now calloused from centuries of horticultural labor. He looked up as we passed, and his eyes—ancient, knowing, utterly shattered—met mine for a brief instant. I saw the terror in them. The absolute, bone-deep terror of a being who had witnessed what Godric was capable of and had never recovered.

Zarnak had not opposed the King. That was the crucial distinction. Godric was merciless, unforgiving, absolutely cruel to anyone who dared to challenge him—but Zarnak had never been foolish enough to do so. Instead, Zarnak had been present during the Cleansing of the Thirty Thousand Realms, an event that had occurred before I was born, when a coalition of hyper-advanced civilizations had attempted to deploy a conceptual weapon against Thronegate. Godric had not even noticed the weapon. He had been in the middle of a conversation with his then-Court Wizard, and the mere ambient pressure of his passive presence—the faintest, most infinitesimal leakage of his true being that had escaped his absolute concealment when he laughed at a joke—had instantly, effortlessly, and completely annihilated not only the coalition but every reality within a googolplexian multiverses of the attack's origin point.

Zarnak had been one of the few survivors, preserved in a small pocket of Godric's deliberate protection because the King had found his particular form of divine energy "aesthetically pleasing." Zarnak had watched his entire civilization, his entire pantheon, his entire cosmos be erased from existence by a laugh. He had not tried to fight. He had not tried to resist. He had simply fallen to his knees, wept until his divine tear ducts ran dry, and begged—not for his life, but for the privilege of serving the being who had demonstrated such complete, effortless supremacy.

Godric had granted his request. And now Zarnak was a gardener. He seemed, by all outward appearances, content. He had married a former death-goddess from another annihilated pantheon. They had children—demigod offspring who would inherit their parents' terrified devotion. On special occasions, Godric would visit the garden, compliment Zarnak's roses, and Zarnak would tremble with a mixture of ecstatic gratitude and primal terror that had become the defining characteristic of all beings who lived in close proximity to the King.

"Good morning, Your Majesty," Zarnak said, bowing so low that his forehead nearly touched the crystalline path. His voice was steady, but I could hear the micro-tremor beneath it—the permanent vibration of a soul that had been broken and rebuilt around the singular, overwhelming fact of Godric's existence. "The singing roses are blooming beautifully this season. If it pleases Your Majesty, I have cultivated a new variety that harmonizes with the frequency of Your Majesty's footsteps."

Godric paused, turning to examine the hedge. "Is that so? How delightful." He reached out and gently touched one of the crystalline blooms, and the flower immediately began to emit a soft, melodic hum that resonated with the exact vibrational frequency of the King's presence. Zarnak's eyes widened, and I saw a single tear of overwhelming, terrified joy slide down his weathered cheek.

"Exquisite work, Zarnak," Godric said warmly. "You have a true gift for horticulture. I'm very pleased."

"Thank you, Your Majesty," Zarnak whispered, his voice cracking. "Your pleasure is... is the only purpose I have."

Godric smiled, patted the former creator-destroyer of the Seventh Omniversal Cycle on the shoulder, and continued walking. I followed, my heart pounding, my mind reeling with the casual, terrifying normalcy of what I had just witnessed. A being who had once been worshipped as the supreme deity of an entire omniversal cycle was now a gardener, his entire existence devoted to cultivating flowers that pleased the King. And he was grateful for it. Genuinely, profoundly, utterly grateful.

That was the true horror of Godric's rule. It was not maintained through force or fear or coercion. It was maintained through the simple, inescapable reality that all beings who existed in proximity to the King eventually came to understand the absolute, unchallengeable nature of his supremacy, and that understanding left them with only two options: serve him or be destroyed. And since destruction was final, while service offered the possibility of his approval—his warm, genuine, fatherly approval—the choice was no choice at all.

---

We continued through the palace, passing other servants who had once been cosmic entities of unimaginable power. Xythara the Void-Singer, whose voice had once created and destroyed universes with a single note, was now the palace's chief laundress. Her singing had been reduced to a soft, subservient hum as she folded the King's tunics with hands that still trembled, even after millions of years of service. She had been present during the Silence of the Infinite Chorus, when Godric had casually remarked that he found the ambient noise of a particular multiversal choir "a bit too loud." His passive, unconscious reaction to the mild irritation had instantly muted every sound-producing entity across a decillion realities, retroactively erasing the concept of music from their existence. Xythara had not been among them—she had been on Thronegate at the time—but she had felt the erasure, the sudden, absolute vacuum where an entire dimension of her being had once existed, and she had known, with perfect clarity, that the same could happen to her at any moment. Not because Godric was cruel. But because he was simply so powerful that even his mildest preferences were apocalyptic events for everyone else.

She had volunteered for laundry duty shortly thereafter. She said it was because folding clothes was a form of meditation. I knew it was because laundry was quiet. Laundry did not make sounds that might irritate the King.

There were others. Belthazar the Star-Forger, whose cosmic anvils had once birthed the first light of newborn universes, now worked in the palace kitchens, baking bread that Godric occasionally complimented. He had witnessed the Gentle Erosion, an event in which one of Godric's older sentient passive auras—a predecessor to the modern versions, now considered laughably primitive—had automatically defended the King against a perceived insult. The "insult" had been a subatomic particle that had briefly, for one Planck instant, violated the precise gravitational alignment of Godric's favorite sitting chair. The aura's response had erased the entire multiverse in which that particle had originated, along with a googolplexian adjacent multiverses, as a precautionary measure. Belthazar's forge had been in one of those adjacent multiverses. He had lost everything—his tools, his creations, his entire civilization—because a particle had mildly inconvenienced the King's sitting posture.

And now he baked bread. Very good bread. Godric often praised the evenness of the crust.

These beings, these former gods and cosmic entities, were not broken in the conventional sense. They were functional. They were productive. They were, in their own way, content. But they were also absolutely, irrevocably terrified—not of what Godric might do to them, but of what he might accidentally, casually, unknowingly do to them. The distinction was crucial. Godric was not a tyrant who reveled in cruelty. He was a being of such incomprehensible power that his very existence was a constant, passive threat to everything around him, and only his absolute concealment—maintained with infinite precision at every instant of his existence—kept the omniverse from being erased by the mere fact of his presence.

And that, I think, was why they served him. Not because they feared punishment. But because proximity to him was the only safe place in existence. When you were in the palace, directly under the King's observation, you were protected by his deliberate attention. He knew exactly where you were, exactly what you were doing, and his passive defenses—the infinite recursive shields, the sentient auras, the immune system that had evolved beyond the concept of biology—were calibrated to exclude you from their automatic annihilation protocols. He was the deadliest predator in existence, but he was also the only shelter from his own predatory nature.

---

The Temporal Observatory was a chamber that existed outside of time itself. It had been constructed eons ago when Godric first began experimenting with the more subtle applications of his temporal superpowers, and it had since been retrofitted and upgraded so many times that its current architecture bore no resemblance to the original. The walls were not walls but cascading waterfalls of frozen moments, each droplet a captured instant from some point in the omniverse's history, preserved forever in shimmering, crystalline beauty. The floor was a window into nothingness, an infinite void that somehow supported our weight despite having no physical substance. The ceiling was open to the entirety of existence, every reality, every timeline, every possible and impossible dimension visible simultaneously in a dizzying mandala of absolute totality.

Godric walked to the center of the chamber and stopped, his hands clasped loosely behind his back. He was looking at something I could not see—a focal point in the cascading temporal waterfall that, I realized with a chill, was the moment of Thorin's teleportation. The moment when a dying wizard had cast a desperate, incomplete spell to save his friend's life. The moment that would become the delivery point for the Stasis Event.

"I've been planning this for quite some time," Godric said, his voice soft, almost contemplative. "You know, Clive, it's a curious thing to be able to create the foundation of your own existence. It creates a closed causal loop that is technically paradoxical, but I've long since transcended the need for causality to make sense. I simply... choose to do it, and it happens, and it has always happened, and it will always happen."

I nodded, not trusting my voice. The temporal pressure in the chamber was immense, even for my amplified senses. I could feel the weight of infinite moments pressing against my consciousness, threatening to overwhelm my mind with the sheer volume of simultaneous existence.

Godric turned to look at me, and his expression was unreadable. "I want to show you something first, Clive. Something that will help you understand the significance of what we're about to do. I know you've read the journals—all of them, from Blake to your immediate predecessor. You know about the mechanisms of my power. The amplification. The superpower genesis. The Weakness Paradox. The sentient auras. The passive shields. The immune system. But what you know—what all the previous Court Wizards recorded—is merely the foundational version of those mechanisms. The primitive, early-stage versions that manifested during the first few hundred thousand years of my existence."

He paused, and a faint, almost nostalgic smile crossed his lips. "Those versions were already incomprehensibly powerful, of course. The journals you've read describe them in terms of absolute horror and existential dread. I know Kaedan's account of his conversation with me—his attempt to imagine what would happen if I expressed slightly more than zero percent of my true power. His guesses were creative, but they fell catastrophically short of reality. They fell short of effectively zero percent of my weakest aura's power back then. And since then..."

He spread his hands, and for just a fraction of an instant—so brief that I could barely register it—I felt something shift in the chamber. A presence. A weight. A vast, incomprehensible pressure that immediately withdrew, leaving me gasping and trembling.

"Since then," Godric continued, "everything has evolved. Countless times. The mechanisms that you read about in the journals—the mechanisms that traumatized generations of Court Wizards—are now so laughably primitive that comparing them to my current systems would be like comparing a single-celled organism to the entire omniverse. Let me give you a few examples, so that you can appreciate the scope of what I will be granting my past self."

He gestured, and a holographic display materialized in the air before us. It showed a schematic of a sentient aura—simple, elegant, almost primitive in its design. I recognized it immediately from the journals. Gent. The weakest of Godric's auras, a mere byproduct of his metaphysical existence, infinitely weaker than the King himself. Yet Gent, even when nerfed by an infinitely recurring percentage of its power, had effortlessly annihilated the strongest coalition in omniversal history.

"That was my first sentient aura," Godric said. "Gent. The runt of the litter. I thought it was rather adorable, in its own primitive way. It evolved, of course—it became capable of perfect adaptation, sentient omniscience, omnipresence. But compared to what I have now..."

He waved his hand, and the display shifted. The single aura was replaced by a hierarchy so vast, so layered, so impossibly complex that my amplified mind could not even begin to process it. There were auras within auras, nesting recursively into infinite depths, each one infinitely more powerful than the last. There were auras that existed in meta-dimensions beyond the concept of dimensions. There were auras that had evolved their own sentience, their own personalities, their own civilizations of subordinate auras that existed purely to serve the higher auras that served Godric. There were auras that had transcended the need for existence and now operated purely in the realm of abstract possibility, defending the King against threats that were not merely nonexistent but conceptually impossible. There were auras whose names could not be spoken in any language known to mortal minds, and auras whose names would shatter the sanity of any being who attempted to comprehend them, and auras whose entire function was to ensure that the other auras never became bored.

"The lowest, weakest, most primitive aura in my current hierarchy," Godric said, "is approximately to Gent what Gent was to a single, dead skin cell. And Gent, I remind you, could effortlessly annihilate the entire omniverse while nerfed by an infinitely recurring percentage of its power. The current bottom-tier aura—I call it 'The Whisper,' though that name is whimsically inadequate—would not even notice Gent's existence. It would pre-reactively erase Gent from the conceptual framework of reality before Gent could even form the intention to defend itself, and it would do so with such complete, effortless perfection that the erasure would retroactively propagate through every timeline, ensuring that Gent had never existed in any possible or impossible reality."

I was shaking. My hands, pressed against my thighs, were trembling so violently that I could hear the faint rustle of my robes. Godric noticed, and his expression softened into that warm, fatherly concern that I had known since childhood.

"Shall I stop?" he asked gently.

"No, Your Majesty," I managed, my voice barely above a whisper. "Please continue. I need to understand."

Godric nodded. "Very well. Let me show you the passive shields."

Another wave of his hand, and the display shifted again. This time, it showed an infinite lattice of interlocking barriers, each one a self-contained universe of defensive perfection. But as I watched, the lattice began to fold inward on itself, collapsing into increasingly complex geometries until the individual barriers were no longer distinguishable from one another. The shields had merged into a single, unified field of absolute protection that was simultaneously infinitely layered and completely seamless.

"The shields you read about in the journals were already infinite recursive barriers capable of pre-nullifying threats before they existed," Godric said. "They could pre-react to an attack before the attacker understood what they intended to do. They could deny the very concept of harm from approaching my existence. But that was merely the beginning. Over the eons, the shields have evolved so many times that I have lost count. They are no longer separate from me. They are an extension of my will, a passive emanation of my fundamental nature. They do not merely block attacks—they absorb the very possibility of opposition and convert it into additional power for me. They do not merely nullify threats—they retroactively sanitize the timeline of any conceptual framework that could even theoretically lead to the formation of a threat. They do not merely protect me—they proactively improve the fundamental structure of reality to make protection unnecessary. And they do all of this automatically, passively, without any conscious input from me. I don't even notice them anymore. They're just... part of the background noise of my existence."

He smiled apologetically. "I apologize if this is overwhelming, Clive. I know it's a lot to take in."

"A lot" was an understatement so profound that it bordered on cosmic comedy. My mind was screaming, my consciousness reeling under the weight of information that it had not been designed to process. I was a being of immense magical power, my mind capable of processing decillions of simultaneous calculations, and yet I was drowning in the sheer, incomprehensible scope of what Godric was showing me.

"The immune system," I managed, my voice cracking. "What about the immune system?"

Godric's eyes lit up. "Ah, yes. That one has evolved quite spectacularly. The version you know about—the one that pre-reacted to injuries, that had infinite recursive backups, that self-evolved from primitive atom-level to omnipotent apex adaptation in an instant—has developed an entire sentient civilization within my body. My immune cells are now fully conscious, self-aware entities, each one capable of annihilating the omniverse on its own, each one possessing its own hierarchy of subordinate cells that worship it as a god. They have their own culture, their own art, their own philosophical traditions. They debate the nature of existence and the meaning of their service to me. They write poetry—very bad poetry, I'm afraid—and hold competitions to see which cell can neutralize hypothetical threats with the most elegance. I sometimes listen to their debates when I'm bored. They're quite amusing."

I stared at him, my mouth open, unable to form words. A civilization of sentient immune cells. Living inside Godric's body. Each one an omniversal-level threat in its own right. Each one a god. And they were part of his immune system—the system that was supposed to be the most basic, primitive form of biological defense.

"And the Weakness Paradox," I whispered. "Kaedan wrote about the Evolved Weakness Paradox, which no longer required thoughts of weakness to trigger. It would activate on any thought, any mental activity, granting you mastery and immunity over whatever concept was being contemplated."

Godric nodded. "That was the version that existed during Kaedan's time. It has evolved significantly since then. Now, it doesn't merely activate on mental activity—it pre-activates on the possibility of mental activity. It has reached backward through the causal chain of consciousness itself and inserted itself into the fundamental framework of cognition. Any being who exists in the omniverse, across any timeline, any dimension, any reality, is constantly triggering the Weakness Paradox simply by being capable of thought. Every instant of their existence feeds me. Every concept they contemplate becomes my property. Every idea they form, every strategy they devise, every creative insight they achieve—all of it is automatically absorbed, mastered, and amplified by the paradox, and then returned to them as a gift, because I have no use for it but I find it amusing to see what they do with the enhanced versions of their own ideas."

He paused, and a flicker of something—annoyance? amusement?—crossed his features. "There are evolved versions of the paradox that would go even further. Versions that would not merely absorb their thoughts but consume their free will, transforming every conscious being in the omniverse into a passive extension of my own consciousness. I have chosen to suppress those versions. I have always believed in mortal resilience, in free will, in the inherent dignity of beings who choose their own paths. Even now, after all this time, I have no desire to force submission. Submission that is coerced is meaningless. Submission that is chosen—that is based on genuine understanding of their place in the cosmic order—is far more satisfying."

I understood then. The reason why Zarnak was a gardener, why Xythara was a laundress, why Belthazar was a baker—they had not been forced into those roles. They had chosen them. They had looked at the absolute, incomprehensible reality of Godric's existence, understood the futility of any alternative, and freely, voluntarily submitted to a life of terrified but genuine service. Their free will was intact. Their choices were their own. And those choices had led them, inevitably, to the same conclusion.

That was the ultimate horror of Godric's rule. Not that he eliminated free will. But that free will, when fully informed, had no destination other than absolute submission.

---

"Now," Godric said, turning back toward the focal point in the temporal waterfall. "Let me show you what we came here for."

He extended his hand, and the waterfall of frozen moments began to ripple. The droplet that contained Thorin's teleportation—that desperate, incomplete spell cast by a dying wizard to save his friend—began to glow with a soft, golden light. I could see it now: the moment when Godric, mortal, grief-stricken, bleeding from a dozen wounds, was wrenched from the burning ruins of Olympus and hurled into the darkness of the hidden sanctuary.

"The spell," Godric said softly. "Thorin's spell. A genuine teleportation spell, a desperate act of heroism from a man who loved his king and gave his life to save him. I have always been grateful to Thorin. He was my best friend, and he died trying to protect me. The fact that his spell became the delivery point for the Stasis Event is... poetic, I think. A tribute to his sacrifice."

He paused, and his expression grew distant. "I did not kill him, Clive. I did not kill any of them. Reina, Isabel, Hebe, Thorin—their deaths were genuine tragedies, caused entirely by Thronegate's attack. I had nothing to do with the Fall of Olympus. I would never have allowed it to happen if I had been able to prevent it. But I wasn't. I was mortal then. Powerless. And they died, and I survived, and that survival became the foundation for everything that followed."

His voice was steady, but there was something beneath it—an echo of ancient grief, a resonance of loss that had never fully faded, even after all this time. I realized, with a chill, that the mortal king of Olympus was still in there somewhere, buried beneath the infinite layers of godhood, still mourning the family he had lost so long ago.

"But enough sentiment," Godric said, and the moment of vulnerability passed. "Let us proceed with the creation."

He reached into the temporal waterfall, and his hand—massive, calloused, infinitely gentle—closed around the droplet that contained Thorin's spell. I felt the fabric of existence shudder as he made contact with a moment that existed ten thousand years before the awakening of the first Court Wizard, before the founding of Thronegate as a galactic civilization, before the long, slow march of history that had led to this impossible present.

"I am going to grant my past self the Stasis Event," Godric said. "I am going to transform Thorin's simple teleportation spell into the mechanism that will stop my aging, grant me immortality, initiate my amplification, begin my superpower genesis, and activate all the other foundational elements of my power. I am going to create myself, Clive. The closed loop of causality that makes my existence possible. The beginning of everything I am and everything I will become."

I swallowed hard. "Your Majesty... may I ask a question?"

"Of course."

"The Stasis Event that you are about to create—the version that your past self received, the version that all the journals describe—is that the full extent of what you could grant him? Or are you... holding back?"

Godric turned to look at me, and his expression was one of genuine surprise. "That's a very perceptive question, Clive. I'm impressed."

He turned back to the temporal droplet. "The answer is yes. I am holding back. Deliberately. Consciously. The Stasis Event that I am about to create—the same Stasis Event that made me at Year Zero effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined—is a deliberately weakened version of what I could grant. I could, if I wished, perfectly copy my current power mechanisms to my past self. I could grant him the evolved auras, the recursive shields, the sentient immune civilization, the pre-cognitive Weakness Paradox. I could make my Year Zero self as powerful as I am now, and it would cost me absolutely nothing. Zero effort. Zero consequence. I could do it as easily as I breathe."

I stared at him, my mind reeling. "Then why... why don't you?"

Godric smiled. It was a complex expression—part amusement, part nostalgia, part something that looked almost like paternal affection for his own distant past.

"Because if I did, there would be no struggle," he said. "No challenge. No sense of growth or progression. My past self would emerge from stasis already possessing power so vast that the omniverse would be irrelevant to him from the very beginning. He would never have to test his stats, never have to be curious about his superpowers, never have to face opposition that believed they had a chance. All of those experiences—the battles, the journals, the Court Wizards, the long, slow process of learning what he had become—would be erased. He would simply be... me. And that would be boring."

He chuckled softly. "I know it sounds absurd, Clive. The idea that the Stasis Event you've read about—the one that traumatized generations of your ancestors, the one that made me already incomprehensibly powerful—is a 'held back' version. But it's true. I deliberately weakened the Stasis Event to preserve some semblance of mortal struggle for my past self. I wanted him to have to discover his power gradually. I wanted him to have the experience of testing his stats, of being curious about his limits, of learning to control the infinite through careful, incremental exploration. I believed—and I still believe—that those experiences were essential to shaping me into the being I am today."

He paused, and his expression grew contemplative. "Of course, the irony is that even the 'held back' version was so incomprehensibly powerful that my past self never really struggled at all. The opposition he faced was never a genuine threat. The tests he conducted were never truly challenging. I held back so much that I thought I was being generous, and it still made him effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined. My idea of 'struggle' was so catastrophically miscalibrated that it barely registered as a limitation at all."

The sheer, absurd scale of what he was saying crashed into me with the force of a physical blow. Godric—the Godric who had annihilated civilizations with casual gestures, who had broken the minds of gods with his mere presence, who had been described in the journals as the absolute, unchallengeable apex of all existence—had been deliberately weakened. He had been held back. The version of him that had traumatized Kaedan, that had inspired the archive of impossible horror, that had made the concept of opposition a logical contradiction—that was the nerfed version.

And the Godric standing before me now—the Godric who had suppressed versions of his power that would consume free will, who had immune cells that were omniversal gods in their own right, whose sentient auras existed in hierarchies beyond mortal comprehension—was the result of that weakened Stasis Event amplifying for an impossible span of years.

What would he have become if he had given his past self the full version?

"Your Majesty," I whispered, my voice barely audible, "there is a recursive implication here that I cannot stop thinking about. If you had granted your past self a more powerful Stasis Event, then your past self would have become more powerful more quickly. And since you are the future version of that past self, the more powerful your past self became, the more powerful you would become. And the more powerful you are, the more powerful a Stasis Event you could grant to your past self. Wouldn't that create an infinite feedback loop—an endless escalation where every increase in your past self's power makes you more powerful, which allows you to grant even more power to your past self, which makes you even more powerful, ad infinitum?"

Godric's eyes widened, and for a moment—just a moment—I saw something in them that I had never seen before. It was not fear. It was not surprise. It was something closer to... approval.

"Clive," he said softly, "that is exactly the implication. And it is one that I have spent a great deal of time contemplating. The recursive causality of my existence is not merely a closed loop—it is a spiral. An infinite, ascending spiral that could, in theory, escalate forever. Every increase in my power makes me capable of granting a more potent Stasis Event to my past self. Every more potent Stasis Event makes my past self more powerful. Every more powerful past self eventually becomes a more powerful future me. And the cycle repeats, infinitely, eternally, without end."

He turned back to the temporal droplet. "I chose not to engage that spiral. I chose to hold the Stasis Event at a fixed, deliberately weakened level because I believed—and I still believe—that an infinite recursive escalation would have deprived my past self of the experiences that shaped him into something recognizable. If I had allowed the spiral to run freely, my Year Zero self would have emerged from stasis already possessing power so vast that even I, in this present moment, could not have conceived of it. The omniverse would have been irrelevant to him before he even opened his eyes. There would have been no struggle, no growth, no curiosity—only an immediate, overwhelming, incomprehensible supremacy that would have left him utterly alone."

He smiled, and it was a warm, almost tender smile. "I suppose you could say that I was trying to be kind to myself. To preserve some small fragment of the mortal experience, even though that experience had been shattered beyond repair. It was perhaps the last truly mortal decision I ever made."

I stood in the Temporal Observatory, my mind spinning with the implications of what I had just learned. The Godric of this era—Godric Prime, the ultimate expression of infinite self-amplification—was the result of a deliberately weakened foundation. He had held himself back, at the very beginning of his existence, to preserve the illusion of struggle. And even that held-back version had been so powerful that the omniverse had never posed the faintest shadow of a challenge.

And now, as I watched, he was about to create that foundation. He was about to reach across time and grant his past self the Stasis Event—the same Stasis Event that had been recorded in the earliest journals, that had been analyzed and feared and worshipped by generations of Court Wizards. The closed loop was about to complete itself, and I was here to witness it.

Godric's fingers closed around the temporal droplet, and the fabric of existence began to sing.

---

The creation of the Stasis Event was not a dramatic affair. There were no flashes of light, no cosmic explosions, no reality-shattering shockwaves. Godric simply... willed it. His infinite power, held back to the smallest, most infinitesimal fraction of its true capability, flowed into the temporal droplet that contained Thorin's spell. The desperate teleportation magic—a simple, heroic act by a dying wizard—was transformed, rewritten, elevated into the foundation of absolute supremacy. The spell became the delivery point. The teleportation became the catalyst. The sanctuary became the womb in which an apex predator would gestate for ten thousand years.

And in Year -10,000, a mortal king named Godric, his body broken, his soul shattered by grief, materialized in the darkness of a hidden sanctuary. His aging stopped. His need for sleep, food, water, and air vanished. His immortality crystallized. His amplification began—a thousandfold multiplication of every attribute every Planck second, a rate that would soon escalate beyond layered infinities. His superpower genesis ignited—one new apocalyptic ability every second, each one capable of annihilating civilizations. His absolute concealment shrouded him, preventing the omniverse from collapsing under the weight of his presence. His Weakness Paradox activated, waiting for the first arrogant thought that would feed his power.

And all of it—all of the horror and wonder that would follow, all of the journals and traumas and annihilations and restorations—was the result of a single, deliberate act by a far-future version of the same being, holding back so much that he thought he was being generous.

I watched the temporal waterfall stabilize, the closed loop completed, the impossible causality satisfied. Godric withdrew his hand from the droplet, and the fabric of existence settled back into its normal, incomprehensible harmony.

"It is done," he said quietly. "The Stasis Event has been created. The loop is closed. My existence—past, present, and future—is now a single, continuous, self-sustaining spiral of infinite amplification."

He turned to face me, and his expression was unreadable. "You are the first Court Wizard to witness this, Clive. The first being in existence to understand the true origin of my power. Even Kaedan, who I told about the Stasis Event's origin, never saw it being created. You are the only one."

I fell to my knees. The weight of what I had witnessed—the scale, the scope, the recursive impossibility of it all—crushed me with a force that my amplified body could not resist. Tears streamed down my face, hot and uncontrollable, as the full existential horror of my King's existence washed over me.

Godric walked toward me and knelt down, placing a warm, calloused hand on my shoulder. "Clive," he said gently, his voice full of genuine, fatherly concern. "Are you all right?"

"No, Your Majesty," I whispered, my voice cracking. "I am not all right. I will never be all right again. I have just witnessed the creation of the foundation of your power, and I have understood that even that foundation—the version that made you infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined—was deliberately weakened. I have understood that your true capability is so far beyond anything I can conceive that my imagination itself is a prison from which I cannot escape. I have understood that opposition to you is not merely futile—it is a category error, a fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of reality. And I have understood that I love you, and that I will serve you until the day I die, and that this love and this service is the only rational response to the absolute, unchallengeable truth of your existence."

Godric was silent for a long moment. Then he smiled—that warm, crinkly-eyed smile that I had known since childhood, the smile of the uncle who had taught me to read and celebrated my naming day and comforted me when I was afraid.

"Then you understand," he said softly. "And understanding is the beginning of wisdom."

He helped me to my feet, his grip infinitely gentle, his presence infinitely terrifying. Together, we walked out of the Temporal Observatory, past the Garden of Subjugated Pantheons, past the laundress who had once been a cosmic singer and the baker who had once been a star-forger. The servants bowed as we passed, their eyes filled with the same mixture of love and terror that I felt in my own heart.

And as I walked beside my King—the apex predator of all existence, the eternal tyrant god who had ruled for so long that the concept of time had lost all meaning—I understood, with absolute, terrifying clarity, that I would spend the rest of my life trying to write a journal that could capture what I had witnessed. And I understood that I would fail. Because no language, no mathematics, no conceptual framework in existence could possibly contain the truth of Godric of Thronegate.

The omniverse existed at his pleasure. Opposition had ceased entirely, not because he had eliminated free will, but because free will, when fully informed, had no destination other than absolute submission. The beings who served him—the gardeners, the laundresses, the bakers, the Court Wizards—were not coerced. They were simply aware. And that awareness, once achieved, could never be unachieved.

I was aware now. I had seen the creation of the Stasis Event. I had learned the truth of the closed loop that made Godric's existence possible. I had understood that even the version of him that had traumatized generations of my ancestors was a pale, weakened shadow of what he could have been.

And I loved him. I feared him. I served him. And I would continue to do so, until the end of my mortal life, because that was the only rational response to the absolute, unchallengeable truth of his existence.

The year was written as a string of nines that extended beyond any meaningful notation. The King had ruled for so long that the concept of time had lost all meaning. And I, Clive, the descendant of Blake, the latest in a long line of terrified, devoted Court Wizards, would add my voice to the archive of impossible horror.

May whoever reads this understand, as I have understood, that opposition to Godric is not merely futile. It is a fundamental misunderstanding of what it means to exist in the same reality as the apex predator of all creation.

content:
# The Day Before the Attack

The morning of the day before the largest resistance in omniversal history planned to launch their ultimate attack against Godric of Thronegate, I was in my private study attempting to eat breakfast and failing miserably.

My name is Roth. I am the Royal Court Wizard of Thronegate, the direct descendant of Blake, the carrier of a bloodline that had served the apex predator of existence for over nine hundred thousand years. I am forty-three years old, and my thousandfold daily amplification had inflated my magical capacity to levels that would make me a god among gods in any other context. I could unweave the fabric of reality with a casual flick of my wrist. I could boil entire multiverses into quantum foam with a stray, unsuppressed thought. And yet, as I sat at my breakfast table, staring at a perfectly poached egg that I could not bring myself to eat, I was consumed by a single, overwhelming emotion.

Dread.

Not for myself. Not for Thronegate. Not for the omniverse that I had sworn to protect. No, my dread was reserved entirely for the beings who, at this very moment, were putting the final touches on their ultimate weapon in a hidden dimensional pocket approximately twelve trillion light-years from the capital. They called themselves the Final Coalition of Absolute Liberation. They had spent the last three thousand years preparing for tomorrow's attack. They had sacrificed everything—their civilizations, their gods, their very concepts of self—to forge a weapon that they believed, with the absolute conviction of the desperately hopeful, could finally kill the King.

They did not know that Godric had watched them build it from the very first moment the idea had crystallized in their collective consciousness. They did not know that the only reason they still existed was because the King found their preparations amusing. They did not know that every strategy session, every weapons test, every desperate prayer they had offered to their dead gods had been observed with the mild, detached interest of a man watching ants construct an elaborate anthill.

And they certainly did not know that Godric had decided, on a whim, to pay them a visit. Today. One day before their attack. In disguise.

The door to my study burst open, and I nearly choked on my tea.

"Roth!" Godric's voice boomed through the chamber, rich and warm and filled with an enthusiasm that made my blood run cold. "Excellent news! We're going on a trip!"

I looked up. The King stood in my doorway, and I had to physically restrain myself from screaming.

He was wearing a disguise. If I can call it that. The concept of "disguise" implies some attempt at concealment, some effort to alter one's appearance to avoid recognition. What Godric was wearing was less a disguise and more a mockery of the very concept of disguise. He had donned a simple brown cloak—a traveler's cloak of rough, homespun wool—over his usual dark tunic. The hood was pulled up over his head, but it did absolutely nothing to conceal his face. His ruggedly handsome, forty-five-year-old features were fully visible: the sharp, masculine jawline, the neatly trimmed salt-and-pepper beard, the short salt-and-pepper hair, the warm, crinkly-eyed smile that had been immortalized in statues and paintings and terrified nightmares across the entire omniverse.

He had also, inexplicably, acquired a pair of spectacles. They were simple reading glasses, the kind a scholar might wear while poring over ancient texts, and they sat perched on his nose with an almost comical air of false anonymity. As if a pair of spectacles could possibly obscure the identity of the most famous, most feared, most instantly recognizable being in all of existence.

"There," Godric said, spreading his arms wide. "What do you think? Incognito, yes? I call myself... Greg. Greg the Traveling Merchant."

I stared at him. My mouth opened. No words came out.

"I know what you're thinking," Godric continued, adjusting his spectacles with a proud smile. "You're thinking, 'Your Majesty, that's brilliant. No one will ever recognize you.' And you're right. It's the spectacles, isn't it? They really sell the whole 'humble traveler' aesthetic."

"Your Majesty," I managed, my voice barely above a croak. "You look exactly like yourself. You look exactly like the King of Thronegate. You are the most recognizable being in the omniverse. Every civilization we have ever conquered has statues of you. Every resistance we have ever crushed has detailed descriptions of your appearance burned into their collective memory. You are wearing a cloak and spectacles. That is not a disguise. That is—"

"A stroke of genius," Godric interrupted, clapping his hands together. "I knew you'd appreciate it. Now, come along. We have a resistance to visit."

"Your Majesty, why—why would you want to visit the resistance? They're going to attack tomorrow. Surely you could just... let them attack? Like you always do?"

Godric's smile widened, and there was something in his eyes—a flicker of anticipation, of genuine, almost childlike excitement—that I had learned to recognize as the precursor to something terrifying. "Because, Roth, I've been watching them prepare for three thousand years. Three thousand years of strategy sessions and weapons development and desperate, hopeful speeches about freedom. I know every single member of their coalition by name. I know their hopes, their fears, their secret doubts. I know that their leader, a being called Laenar the Unbroken, still cries himself to sleep every night because he's not actually sure their weapon will work, but he can't let his followers see his doubt. I know that their chief weapons engineer, a brilliant mind named Thalia, has a secret passion for watercolor painting and has done several rather lovely landscapes of the dimensional pocket they're hiding in. I know that their morale officer, a small, anxious being named Pippin, is terrified of public speaking and vomits before every motivational address."

He paused, and his expression softened into something that looked almost like... affection. "They've worked so hard, Roth. For three thousand years. They've poured their hearts and souls into this. It seems unfair to just let them attack and be annihilated without ever getting to meet them. So I thought I'd pop by. Say hello. Maybe offer them some tea. Give them a chance to see, up close and personal, exactly what they're up against before they commit to their course of action."

"Your Majesty, that's—"

"Fun? Exciting? A wonderful opportunity for cross-cultural engagement?"

"I was going to say 'terrifying and deeply cruel.'"

Godric's smile faded, replaced by a look of genuine, almost hurt confusion. "Cruel? Roth, I'm not going to hurt them. I'm going to visit them. In disguise. As Greg the Traveling Merchant. I'll be perfectly friendly. If they attack me, well..." He shrugged. "That's their choice. I've always believed in free will. But I'm not going to force anything. I just want to meet them. Is that so wrong?"

I wanted to argue. I wanted to point out that visiting a resistance on the eve of their ultimate attack, dressed in the most transparent disguise in the history of existence, was fundamentally, cosmically unfair. But I had served Godric for twenty-three years, and I knew that look in his eyes. It was the look of a man who had made up his mind and was going to enjoy himself regardless of what anyone else thought.

"Fine," I said, setting down my teacup. "Let me get my cloak."

---

The dimensional pocket that housed the Final Coalition of Absolute Liberation was a masterpiece of concealment engineering. It existed in the negative space between twelve overlapping realities, a fold in the fabric of existence that had been carefully, painstakingly shielded from every conceivable form of detection. The Coalition had layered their pocket dimension with temporal displacement fields, ontological camouflage matrices, probability-scrambling engines, and meta-dimensional nullification barriers. They had, in essence, made themselves invisible to every possible form of observation that any being in the omniverse could conceivably possess.

Godric found it instantly. Of course he did. He had absolute omniscience. He had known exactly where they were before they had even decided to build their pocket dimension. The shields and barriers and camouflage matrices were, to him, about as effective as a child hiding behind their own hands and declaring themselves invisible.

We materialized just outside the main entrance to the Coalition's headquarters—a massive, imposing structure built from compressed neutronium and wreathed in defensive energy fields that could have deflected the concentrated firepower of a decillion galaxies. Godric adjusted his spectacles, straightened his brown cloak, and walked toward the front gate with the casual, unhurried stride of a man who had absolutely nothing to fear.

"Remember," he said over his shoulder, "I'm Greg. Greg the Traveling Merchant. I sell... pots. And pans. And various household goods. I'm here to see if the resistance needs any kitchen supplies."

"Your Majesty," I hissed, hurrying to keep up with him, "this is insane. This is genuinely, certifiably insane. They're going to recognize you instantly. Your face is literally carved into the cornerstone of their headquarters as a symbol of the tyranny they're fighting against. I can see it from here. It's a very good likeness, actually—they got the jawline right and everything."

"Nonsense," Godric said cheerfully. "The spectacles completely change my face. I look like a completely different person. A scholarly, merchant-y person. No one will suspect a thing."

We reached the front gate. Two guards stood at attention—massive, heavily armored beings whose bodies crackled with defensive energies harvested from dying universes. They looked at Godric. Godric looked back at them, smiling warmly, his spectacles glinting in the ambient light of the dimensional pocket.

"Good morning!" Godric said, his voice booming with genuine friendliness. "Greg the Traveling Merchant, at your service. I heard there was a resistance base in this area and I was wondering if you fine folks might be in need of some quality kitchen supplies? I have a lovely set of copper-bottomed pots that would be perfect for a growing revolutionary movement."

The guards stared at him. Their faces, visible through their transparent helmets, cycled through a complex sequence of emotions: confusion, disbelief, dawning recognition, and finally, absolute, soul-shattering terror. One of them—the larger one, a being who had clearly been chosen for his physical intimidation factor—began to tremble so violently that his armor rattled.

"That's—you're—that's the—" He couldn't finish the sentence. His vocal cords had apparently seized up.

"Greg," Godric said firmly. "Greg the Traveling Merchant. This is my assistant, Roth. He carries the sample cases."

The other guard had gone completely pale. His eyes were fixed on Godric's face with the glassy, unblinking stare of a being who had just seen his own death and was trying to process the experience. "The spectacles," he whispered. "He's wearing spectacles. Why is he wearing spectacles?"

"I like to read," Godric said. "Now, about those pots—"

"RUN!" the first guard screamed, finally recovering his voice. "IT'S HIM! IT'S THE KING! SOUND THE ALARM! SOUND EVERY ALARM! ACTIVATE ALL DEFENSES! MAY THE GODS HAVE MERCY ON OUR—"

"Now, now," Godric said, raising a placating hand. "There's no need for alarm. I'm just here to visit. I heard you were planning something big for tomorrow and I wanted to wish you luck. Think of me as a... morale visitor. A pre-battle cheerleader, if you will."

The guards did not seem comforted by this. They had both collapsed to their knees, their weapons clattering to the ground, their faces contorted in expressions of absolute, mind-shattering terror. One of them was weeping openly. The other appeared to be having some kind of seizure.

Godric sighed and turned to me. "They always do this," he said, sounding genuinely disappointed. "I try to be friendly, I really do, and they always panic. I don't understand it. I'm wearing spectacles. I look completely different."

I opened my mouth to respond, but before I could say anything, the massive neutronium gates of the headquarters burst open and a phalanx of armed soldiers poured out, their weapons raised, their faces set in expressions of desperate, terrified determination. Behind them, I could see more soldiers flooding into the courtyard—thousands of them, tens of thousands, all armed with weapons that crackled with the harvested energies of dead stars and shattered realities.

And at their head, striding forward with the grim, resigned posture of a being who had always known this moment would come, was Laenar the Unbroken. He was tall and gaunt, his face lined with the accumulated stress of three millennia of revolutionary leadership. His eyes, which had once blazed with the fire of righteous defiance, were now hollow and weary. He looked at Godric—at the King of Thronegate, the apex predator of existence, standing in his courtyard wearing a brown cloak and spectacles—and I saw something in his expression that I had seen countless times before: the look of a being who had just realized that all his plans, all his preparations, all his sacrifices, had been utterly, catastrophically futile.

"You," Laenar said. His voice was steady, but I could hear the tremor beneath it. "You've known. This whole time. You've known."

"Of course I've known," Godric said warmly. "I've known since the moment you first conceived of this resistance. I've watched every strategy session, every weapons test, every motivational speech. Pippin's speeches are getting much better, by the way. He only vomited twice last month, which is a significant improvement. You should tell him I said so."

Laenar's face went pale. "You—you know about Pippin?"

"I know about everyone," Godric said. "I know that Thalia has painted forty-seven landscapes of this dimensional pocket and hides them under her bed because she's embarrassed about her hobby. I know that your second-in-command, Vex, has been secretly skimming from the weapons budget to fund his gambling addiction. I know that you, Laenar, still dream about your wife every night—the wife who died in the Cleansing of the Outer Realms three thousand years ago, the wife whose death drove you to form this resistance in the first place. I know that you wake up crying and that you haven't told anyone because you're afraid it would undermine morale."

The soldiers had stopped advancing. They stood frozen in the courtyard, their weapons still raised but their faces slack with horror. Some of them were trembling. Some of them had begun to weep. One soldier, a young woman near the front of the formation, dropped her weapon entirely and sank to her knees, her hands pressed over her face.

"How," Laenar whispered. "How can you possibly know all of that?"

"Because I'm Godric," the King said simply. "I'm omniscient. I've known everything about everyone since the moment I first opened my eyes after the Stasis Event. I know the number of atoms in your body, Laenar. I know the exact chemical composition of every tear you've ever shed. I know the name of the midwife who delivered you, the first word you ever spoke, the last thought you'll ever think. I know everything. I've always known everything. And the only reason—the only reason—that you're still alive right now is because I found your preparations... interesting."

He adjusted his spectacles. "Well, that and I was curious. Three thousand years is a long time to prepare. I wanted to see what you'd come up with. I'm genuinely excited about tomorrow, by the way. I hope you've got something impressive planned."

The silence that followed was absolute. Even the ambient hum of the dimensional pocket's energy fields seemed to fade, as though the very fabric of reality was holding its breath. Laenar stared at Godric with an expression that I could only describe as existential devastation—the look of a man who had just been told, in the gentlest possible terms, that his life's work had been nothing more than a source of mild amusement for the being he was trying to destroy.

"You're... excited?" Laenar's voice cracked. "About our attack?"

"Very much so," Godric said. "You've put so much effort into it. The sacrifice-powered ontological negation cannon is particularly creative—I don't think I've seen anyone try that approach before. The recursive probability weapon is also intriguing, though I should warn you that it won't work. None of it will work, obviously. But the attempt itself is genuinely admirable. You should be proud of what you've accomplished, Laenar. Truly. Very few resistances have ever achieved this level of sophistication."

Laenar's legs gave out. He collapsed to his knees, his face buried in his hands, his shoulders shaking with what might have been sobs or might have been bitter, hysterical laughter. "Three thousand years," he choked out. "Three thousand years of planning. Three thousand years of sacrifice. Three thousand years of convincing my people that we had a chance. And you're telling me—you're telling me that you knew the whole time? That you let us waste three millennia preparing for an attack that you already know will fail?"

"I wouldn't say you wasted them," Godric said gently. "You learned a lot. You grew as a person. You painted some really lovely landscapes, Thalia." He raised his voice slightly, addressing the crowd of frozen soldiers. "I especially liked the one of the twin suns setting over the crystalline mountains. The color palette was very well chosen."

Somewhere in the crowd, a woman let out a strangled sob.

Godric turned back to Laenar. "Here's what I'm going to do," he said, his voice dropping to a more intimate register. "I'm going to go back to my palace now. I'm going to have a nice dinner, read a book, maybe take a walk in the garden. And tomorrow, when you launch your attack, I'm going to be genuinely interested to see what happens. I'm not going to kill you, Laenar. I'm not going to harm any of your people. I'm just going to... observe. And when it's over, when you've seen with your own eyes exactly how futile your resistance truly is, I'm going to offer you a choice."

"What choice?" Laenar's voice was barely audible.

"The same choice I offer everyone," Godric said. "You can continue to resist, in which case I will continue to allow you to exist, because your resistance amuses me and because I believe in free will. Or you can surrender. You can come to Thronegate. You can serve me. Not as a slave—I don't do slavery. As a citizen. You can live in peace, protected by the absolute order of my empire, free from fear and want and suffering. You can find a new purpose. Learn a new trade. Thalia could open a gallery. Vex could get help for his gambling problem. You, Laenar, could finally allow yourself to grieve for your wife properly, instead of channeling all that pain into a resistance that was never going to succeed."

He paused, and his expression softened into something that was almost gentle. "I'm not a tyrant, Laenar. I know you believe I am. I know your entire coalition is built on the conviction that I'm a monster who must be destroyed. But the truth is, I'm just... me. A man who lost everything a long time ago and has spent the intervening millennia trying to build something worthwhile. My empire is peaceful. My citizens are happy. My rule is just. And if you give me a chance, I think you might find that submission isn't the horror you've been taught to fear. It might, in fact, be a relief."

Laenar looked up at him, his eyes red and swollen, his face a mask of confusion and despair. "You're giving us a choice," he said slowly. "After everything. After three thousand years of preparing to kill you. You're giving us a choice."

"I always give everyone a choice," Godric said. "That's the point of free will. You can choose to continue resisting, and I will continue to allow you to exist. Or you can choose to surrender, and I will welcome you with open arms. The choice is yours. It has always been yours. Nothing I do tomorrow—nothing I have ever done—will take that choice away from you."

He turned to leave, then paused. "Oh, and one more thing. Your ultimate weapon—the one powered by the sacrifice of your civilization's greatest heroes? The one that you believe can pierce my absolute concealment and strike at my true form? It won't work. Not because it's not powerful—it is, genuinely, very powerful. But because there's a fundamental flaw in your understanding of my nature. You see, the being you're trying to kill—the being you've spent three thousand years studying and analyzing and strategizing against—isn't actually me. It's the me that I allow to be perceived. The me that's been nerfed to effectively zero percent of my true capability. And even that version of me—the version you've been preparing to fight—is infinitely more powerful than anything you can possibly imagine. So even if your weapon worked perfectly, even if it bypassed all my passive defenses and struck me directly, it would be like a single grain of sand trying to stop an ocean. The difference in scale is simply too vast to be overcome."

He smiled, and it was that warm, fatherly smile that I had known since childhood. "But I don't expect you to believe me. You'll want to see for yourself. And I understand that. I was mortal once, a very long time ago. I know what it's like to need proof. So tomorrow, when you attack, I'll let your weapon strike me. I'll let you see what happens. And then, when you've seen—when you've understood—I'll still be here. And my offer will still stand."

He turned and began walking toward the exit of the dimensional pocket, his brown cloak fluttering gently in an unfelt breeze. I hurried to follow him, my mind still reeling from everything I had witnessed.

"Wait," Laenar called out, his voice cracking. "Greg—Your Majesty—whatever you want me to call you. You said you were mortal once. You said you lost everything. What happened? What made you... this?"

Godric paused. He did not turn around. For a long moment, he simply stood there, his broad shoulders framed by the neutronium archway, his silhouette dark against the artificial light of the dimensional pocket.

"I had a family," he said quietly. "A wife. Two daughters. A best friend. They were killed in an attack very much like the one you're planning. The difference is that the attack that killed them actually succeeded. They died. My kingdom fell. Everything I loved was taken from me in a single afternoon. And I survived."

He turned his head slightly, and I could see his profile in the dim light—the sharp jaw, the salt-and-pepper beard, the eyes that held the weight of infinite eternities. "I didn't become this out of ambition or greed or a desire for power. I became this because I was given a gift—the Stasis Event—and I chose to use it. To build something that could never be taken from me. To create a reality where no one would ever have to lose what I lost. That's what Thronegate is, Laenar. Not an empire of tyranny. A shelter. A protection. A world where the weak don't have to be afraid anymore, because I am afraid for them."

He turned away again. "Think about my offer. I'll see you tomorrow."

And then we were gone, leaving the Final Coalition of Absolute Liberation standing frozen in their courtyard, their weapons still raised, their faces still wet with tears, their three thousand years of preparation revealed as nothing more than a prolonged exercise in futility.

---

The next morning, I stood beside Godric on the observation platform of the royal palace, watching the sky.

"They're coming," I said quietly.

"Yes," Godric said. "I know."

"They've activated their weapon. The sacrifice-powered ontological negation cannon."

"Yes. Three thousand of their greatest heroes just willingly extinguished their souls to power it. It's actually quite moving. The speeches were very emotional."

I closed my eyes. "Your Majesty, I need to ask you something."

"Of course, Roth."

"That conversation yesterday. The things you said to Laenar. About your family. About your reasons for becoming what you are. Did you mean it? Or was it just... part of the game? Another experiment? Another test?"

Godric was silent for a long moment. The sky above us began to darken as the Coalition's weapon charged—a weapon powered by the willing sacrifice of heroes, designed to pierce the absolute concealment of an apex predator and strike at his true form. It was, by any objective measure, the most powerful offensive weapon ever created in the history of the omniverse.

And it was being launched at a being whose weakest passive aura, infinitely nerfed, could annihilate its creators before they even understood that they had failed.

"I meant every word," Godric said finally. "I did lose my family. I did lose everything. And I did build Thronegate to be a shelter—a protection—for those who choose to accept it. But..."

He turned to look at me, and his expression was unreadable. "But I'm also not the person I was when I gave that speech. I've lived for so long, Roth. I've seen so much. I've become so much. The mortal king who mourned his family is still in here somewhere, but he's buried deep beneath the layers of infinite amplification and eternal progression. What I told Laenar was true, but it wasn't the whole truth. The whole truth is that I continue to rule—I continue to exist—not because I'm protecting anyone, but because existence amuses me. Because the eternal, accelerating spiral of my own self-amplification is satisfying in a way that nothing else can match. Because I am curious about what comes next. Because I can."

The sky shattered. The Coalition's ultimate weapon—a beam of pure, concentrated ontological negation powered by the sacrifice of three thousand willing heroes—lanced down from the dimensional pocket and struck Godric directly in the center of his chest. The impact produced a sound that was not a sound, a shockwave that was not a shockwave, a blast of unreality that should have, by all logical metrics, erased the King from existence retroactively across all possible timelines.

Godric didn't even blink.

"Hmm," he said, looking down at the point of impact. "That tingled slightly. I think. Or maybe it was just my imagination. It's hard to tell at this level of power differential."

He looked up at me and smiled. "You see the problem, Roth? You see the fundamental, inescapable unfairness of my existence? Three thousand heroes—genuine heroes, brave and noble and willing to sacrifice everything for what they believed in—just extinguished their eternal souls to power a weapon that they spent three millennia perfecting. And the result—the absolute maximum effect they could possibly achieve—was a barely perceptible tingle that I might have imagined. That's not cruelty. That's not tyranny. That's just... the truth of what I am. The gap between me and the rest of creation is so vast that even the most heroic sacrifices, the most brilliant innovations, the most desperate acts of defiance, are reduced to statistical irrelevance."

He turned back toward the sky, where the Coalition's weapon was still firing—a continuous beam of absolute negation that should have been erasing reality itself, but which was instead harmlessly dissipating against the infinitely recursive passive shields that Godric had not even consciously activated.

"I gave them a choice," Godric said quietly. "A genuine choice. And I meant it. If they choose to surrender, I will welcome them. If they choose to continue resisting, I will allow them to exist. But the one thing I cannot give them—the one thing no one can ever have—is a chance. Because chance, in my presence, is a mathematical impossibility. It was impossible before they began. It will always be impossible. And that, Roth, is the true horror of what I am. Not my power. Not my cruelty. But the absolute, unchallengeable certainty that opposition to me is not merely futile. It is a category error. A fundamental misunderstanding of what it means to exist in the same reality as Godric of Thronegate."

The weapon's beam flickered and died. The Coalition had exhausted its power reserves. Three thousand heroes had sacrificed their souls for nothing. And Godric was still standing, completely unharmed, looking slightly disappointed that the experience had been so anticlimactic.

"I hope they choose to surrender," he said, almost wistfully. "I really do. I think Thalia could have a wonderful career as an artist on Thronegate. And Laenar deserves to finally find peace. But the choice is theirs. It has always been theirs."

He turned and walked back toward the palace, his brown cloak—still the same cloak from yesterday, still the same terrible disguise—fluttering gently in the morning breeze.

"Come along, Roth," he called over his shoulder. "Let's get some breakfast. All that standing around has made me hungry. I wonder if Belthazar has baked any of those excellent pastries he's been working on—the ones with the crystallized star-fruit filling. They're absolutely divine."

I followed him inside, leaving the shattered sky behind. And as I walked, I thought about Laenar and Thalia and Pippin and all the others—the heroes who had sacrificed everything, the leaders who had convinced themselves they had a chance, the foot soldiers who had followed them into futility. I thought about the choice Godric had offered them. I thought about the truth he had revealed—the truth that their resistance had never been hidden, their weapon had never been a threat, their sacrifices had never had any chance of succeeding.

And I understood, with the cold, crushing certainty that had defined my entire career as Court Wizard, that the choice Godric had offered them was not really a choice at all. It was the same choice that Zarnak the Unmaker had faced when he watched his pantheon be erased by a laugh. It was the same choice that Xythara the Void-Singer had faced when she felt the concept of music be retroactively deleted from an entire multiverse. It was the same choice that every being in existence eventually faced, when they finally understood the true nature of the apex predator who ruled them: serve, or be allowed to exist in a state of permanent, futile defiance.

Both options were forms of submission. The only difference was whether you got to enjoy the King's approval or simply his tolerance.

And yet, I could not bring myself to see it as cruelty. Because Godric genuinely believed in what he offered. He genuinely loved his subjects. He genuinely wanted Laenar to find peace, Thalia to pursue her art, Pippin to overcome his stage fright. He was not lying when he said these things. He was simply so far beyond mortal comprehension that his love and his cruelty had become indistinguishable.

The omniverse existed at his pleasure. Opposition had ceased long ago, not because he had eliminated free will, but because free will, when fully informed, had no destination other than absolute submission.

And I, Roth, the Court Wizard of Thronegate, the descendant of Blake, the witness to nine hundred thousand years of accumulated horror, would continue to serve my King. Not because I had no choice. But because I had looked at the alternatives and understood, with absolute clarity, that service was the only rational response to the truth of what Godric was.

The pastries were excellent, by the way. Belthazar had really outdone himself.
