content:
# A Distant Memory of Pathetic Weakness

The year cannot be written. It cannot be conceived. It cannot be approached by any mathematical notation that mortal or immortal minds have ever devised. The string of nines that represents my reign extends so far beyond comprehensible numeration that even I, in my infinite omniscience, find the exercise of contemplating its full span to be mildly stimulating—a rare sensation, and one I savor when it occurs.

I am Godric. I am the King of Thronegate. I am the apex predator of all existence, the final and ultimate expression of infinite recursive self-amplification, and I have ruled for so long that the concept of "rule" has become merely one of countless abstract notions I permit to exist because their continued presence provides a faint, nostalgic texture to my otherwise absolute experience.

I sit upon a throne that is not a throne but a crystallized moment of perfect supremacy, suspended in a chamber that is not a chamber but a pocket of reality I have shaped to accommodate my momentary preference for architectural nostalgia. The walls are adorned with frozen memories—literal extractions from my own timeline, preserved and mounted like the hunting trophies of a mortal king. Most of them are unremarkable. The subjugation of the Eternal Dynasties. The erasure of the Seven Omniversal Cycles. The gentle correction I applied to the Thirty Thousand Realms when they briefly entertained the notion that collective resistance might yield a different outcome than individual defiance.

But one memory, in particular, draws my attention today. It is old. Ancient, even by my standards—though I use the word "ancient" with the full awareness that all temporal descriptors have long since become arbitrary conveniences. The memory is from Year 25 of my reign. I was barely more than a newborn god at that point, fresh from my conquest of Thronegate, still learning the scope of what the Stasis Event had made me. My power, though already infinite by any objective measure, was so laughably primitive compared to what I am now that the comparison itself feels like a cosmic joke.

And yet—and this is the irony that I find so profoundly amusing—that primitive, infantile version of myself was already so incomprehensibly powerful that an entire universe, brimming with sentient life and desperate hope and the charming conviction that resistance might matter, was reduced to less than nothing in an instant that I deliberately prolonged for my own amusement.

Let me tell you about the day I destroyed Earth.

---

The universe was called the Milky Way by its inhabitants, though I had catalogued it under a far more precise designation in the infinite archives of my omniscience. It was a primitive cosmos by any measure—a single galaxy cluster containing a few hundred billion stars, orbiting a gravitational center that its inhabitants had not yet discovered. The dominant sentient species was a carbon-based bipedal race that called themselves humans. They had existed for approximately three hundred thousand years, had developed basic tool use and symbolic language, and were, at the moment I turned my attention toward them, in the midst of what they charmingly referred to as their "twenty-first century."

I had known about Earth since the instant of my awakening. My omniscience had flooded my consciousness with the complete, total knowledge of every reality, every timeline, every civilization, every atom that existed anywhere in the omniverse. I knew the exact number of grains of sand on every beach of every planet in every galaxy. I knew the name of every human who had ever lived, every thought they had ever thought, every dream they had ever dreamed. I knew the precise chemical composition of the tears shed by a mother in a country called Brazil when her child took its first steps. I knew the exact quantum state of the final breath exhaled by a dying man in a hospital in Tokyo. I knew everything.

And I found them amusing.

Not threatening. Not impressive. Not even particularly interesting. Simply... amusing. The way a toddler's earnest attempt to help with household chores might amuse a parent. They tried so hard, these humans. They built their little civilizations, fought their little wars, composed their little symphonies, and gazed up at their little sky with wonder and terror and desperate hope. They believed themselves to be significant. They believed their struggles mattered. They believed, with the unshakeable conviction of the cosmically naive, that their existence had meaning beyond the fleeting electrical impulses of their primitive neural architecture.

I decided to visit them.

It was Blake who first heard my intention. He was in my private study, reviewing agricultural reports from the outer provinces—I had kept him mortal then, still adjusting to the modified Awakening I had granted him—and when I mentioned that I intended to personally oversee the subjugation of a newly discovered universe, he looked up with that characteristic mixture of loyalty and exasperation that I had come to treasure.

"You're going to terrorize them, aren't you?" he said flatly.

"I'm going to introduce myself," I replied. "There's a difference."

"Is there? For you?"

I considered the question. Blake had always possessed a talent for cutting through my cosmic perspective with the blunt instrument of his mortal honesty. It was one of the reasons I valued him so highly. "Perhaps not," I admitted. "But they have been preparing to resist me. In their own primitive way. Their militaries have detected the approach of Thronegate's expansion front. They've been holding emergency sessions of something called the United Nations. They've activated their nuclear arsenals. They've even attempted to contact me through radio transmissions—very polite transmissions, actually. Several of their leaders have offered unconditional surrender in exchange for mercy."

"Will you give it to them? Mercy?"

I looked at Blake, and I felt the familiar, buried warmth of my mortal self stirring beneath the cold, infinite void that had replaced my heart. "They attempted to develop a weapon," I said quietly. "A biological agent, engineered from something they call CRISPR technology. They theorized that if they could introduce a sufficiently aggressive genetic rewrite into my cells, they might be able to disrupt my amplification. It wouldn't have worked, of course. Even then, my immune system would have annihilated the agent before it came within a trillion light-years of my body. But they tried. They genuinely, sincerely tried to kill me."

Blake was silent for a moment. "And so you're going to kill them."

"I'm going to visit them," I corrected. "What happens after that depends entirely on them."

---

The approach to Earth was deliberately slow. I could have materialized in their atmosphere in zero seconds, of course. I could have simply willed myself into existence above their collective heads and ended the entire affair before their synaptic impulses could register my presence. But where was the fun in that? I was young then—young in the cosmic sense, barely twenty-five years removed from my mortal existence—and I still possessed something that I have long since transcended: a sense of playful mischief.

I wanted them to see me coming. I wanted them to watch their doom approach and understand, with the slow, creeping horror of absolute certainty, that nothing they could do would matter.

So I descended through their solar system at a leisurely pace—"leisurely" meaning approximately one-tenth the speed of light, which to my perception was effectively stationary but to their instruments was a clearly detectable trajectory. I did not hide myself. I did not activate my absolute concealment beyond the baseline suppression that prevented my passive presence from annihilating their galaxy simply by occupying space within it. Their telescopes saw me. Their satellites tracked me. Their military installations calculated my trajectory and projected my arrival time and fed the data to their leaders in a cascade of increasingly panicked transmissions.

The chaos was delightful. I observed it all through my omniscience—the emergency meetings, the tearful phone calls, the world leaders who abandoned their posts and fled to underground bunkers while their populations rioted in the streets. Religious figures of every denomination took to their pulpits and their television networks, some declaring me a demon, others a god, still others a test of faith that would be overcome through righteous devotion. Scientists argued furiously about the nature of my existence, desperately trying to reconcile their understanding of physics with the impossible reality of my approach. Families huddled together in their homes, clutching each other, weeping, praying, waiting.

And still, some of them fought. I had to give them credit for that. Despite everything—despite the clear, undeniable evidence that they were facing a being whose existence defied all known laws of reality—they prepared to resist. Their militaries mobilized. Their nuclear weapons were armed and targeted. Their fighter jets scrambled and formed defensive perimeters. Their most brilliant strategists gathered in war rooms and drew up battle plans that they knew, on some fundamental level, were utterly futile.

I admired their persistence. It was, in its own primitive way, almost noble. But nobility, like all mortal virtues, was merely a prelude to annihilation.

---

I arrived above the city they called New York at precisely 3:47 PM Eastern Standard Time on a Tuesday afternoon. The sky was clear, the sun was bright, and the streets below were filled with the frozen, upturned faces of millions of humans who had stopped in their tracks to stare at the impossible figure descending from the heavens.

I had dressed for the occasion. Not my usual simple dark tunic—that would have been too understated for what I had planned. Instead, I wore the ceremonial armor of Thronegate's early conquest era: a gleaming, obsidian-black breastplate that absorbed light rather than reflecting it, pauldrons carved from the crystallized core of a dead star, and a flowing crimson cape that billowed behind me despite the complete absence of wind. My salt-and-pepper hair was immaculate. My beard was freshly trimmed. My physique, already heavily muscled from my mortal training and now permanently enhanced by the infinite amplification of my strength stat, was displayed to full, terrifying effect.

I looked like a god. Not one of their imagined deities—the bearded patriarchs and radiant angels of their religious iconography—but something older and darker and infinitely more real. A god of absolute, unchallengeable dominion. A god whose very presence was a promise of extinction.

The fighter jets came first. They had been circling at high altitude, waiting for their moment, and when I materialized above the city they descended in a coordinated assault formation that must have taken their strategists weeks to perfect. Forty-two aircraft, each armed with enough firepower to level a small country, converged on my position and unleashed their payloads simultaneously.

The missiles struck me in a cascading wall of fire and shrapnel that would have been genuinely impressive against any opponent who existed within the normal framework of physical reality. The explosions were bright—I'll grant them that. The sound waves generated by the simultaneous detonations shattered windows across the entire eastern seaboard and sent fragments of glass raining down on the streets below like deadly confetti. The heat was sufficient to vaporize steel and ignite the atmosphere in a localized firestorm that consumed the fighter jets themselves, turning their pilots to ash before they could even register that their attack had failed.

Through the flames, I did not move. I did not blink. I did not even register the impact, because the impact—the combined, concentrated firepower of Earth's most advanced military technology—was, relative to the passive resting force of my muscular structure, less than nothing. It was not merely that the missiles failed to harm me. It was that they failed to interact with me on any measurable level whatsoever. The explosions occurred, the shrapnel flew, the pilots died, and I remained exactly as I had been: suspended in midair, arms crossed over my chest, expression of mild, almost bored curiosity on my face.

"Interesting," I said aloud, my voice carrying across the entire planet through the simple expedient of my will. Every human on Earth heard me. Every radio, every television, every digital device simultaneously broadcast my words. "You've put quite a lot of effort into this. The missile guidance systems are particularly sophisticated for a species at your technological level. I'm impressed."

A pause. The flames from the destroyed jets were still billowing around me, black smoke staining the sky above New York. I remained untouched, unmarked, utterly unaffected.

"However, I should inform you that your weapons are not capable of harming me. None of your weapons are capable of harming me. No weapon that exists anywhere in your universe, or any universe, or any conceivable framework of reality, is capable of harming me. I am Godric, King of Thronegate, and I have come to accept your surrender."

Another pause. I could feel their responses through my omniscience—the panic, the disbelief, the desperate, scrambling attempts to formulate a new strategy. Their leaders were shouting at each other through encrypted communication channels. Their generals were demanding options that did not exist. Their scientists were frantically reviewing data that made no sense.

And in a bunker deep beneath the Rocky Mountains, a man whose name I knew—General Marcus Webb, a fifty-seven-year-old military commander with a distinguished career and a failing marriage and a secret fondness for nineteenth-century Russian literature—gave the order to launch the nuclear arsenal.

I smiled. This was going to be fun.

---

The nuclear barrage was, I must admit, genuinely ambitious. They launched everything. Every warhead in every silo, every missile on every submarine, every bomb in every strategic bomber—the entire collective nuclear arsenal of human civilization, directed at a single point in the sky above New York City. The warheads numbered in the thousands, each one capable of destroying an entire metropolitan area, and they converged on my position with the desperate, suicidal precision of a species that had decided that if it was going to die, it would die fighting.

The detonations were simultaneous. The fireball that engulfed me was visible from space, a second sun that briefly outshone the actual sun and bathed the entire western hemisphere in blinding white light. The shockwave propagated outward at supersonic speeds, leveling every structure within a thousand-mile radius, reducing the great cities of the eastern seaboard to smoking rubble, vaporizing millions of humans in the first fraction of a second. The electromagnetic pulse fried every electronic device on the planet, plunging humanity into a sudden, devastating dark age. The atmospheric fallout began to spread, poisoning the air and water, ensuring that even those who survived the initial blast would die slowly and agonizingly in the weeks to come.

And through it all, I remained perfectly still. Perfectly unharmed. Perfectly bored.

"Impressive yield," I said, my voice still carrying effortlessly across the devastated planet. "Your nuclear technology is quite advanced for a species at your developmental stage. The simultaneous detonation strategy was clever—I particularly appreciated the use of submarine-launched missiles to achieve a multi-vector attack pattern. Very creative."

A wet, ragged cough echoed through the silence that followed. One of their leaders—a woman, I believe, though her body was so badly burned that gender identification was difficult—had survived the initial blast by sheltering in a deep underground bunker. She was crawling through the rubble of what had once been the Pentagon, her skin sloughing off her bones in blackened sheets, her lungs filling with superheated ash.

"Why," she gasped, her voice barely audible. "Why are you doing this?"

I descended from the sky and landed softly on the smoldering remains of the building. The heat from the nuclear firestorm was still intense enough to melt steel, but I felt it as a faint, pleasant warmth against my skin—like the sun on a spring afternoon. I walked through the flames and crouched beside the dying woman, my crimson cape pooling around me like a pool of blood.

"You tried to kill me," I said simply. "You developed a biological weapon. You held emergency sessions. You launched your missiles. You did everything in your power to destroy me. And now you ask why?"

She stared up at me with eyes that were already beginning to glaze over. "We were... defending ourselves. You came to... you came to conquer us."

"Yes," I agreed. "I did. And you had a choice. You could have surrendered. Many of your leaders wanted to surrender. But you didn't. You chose to fight. And now—"

I gestured at the burning ruins around us, at the millions of corpses, at the poisoned sky and the shattered planet.

"—now this is what fighting looks like."

She died then. Her heart stopped, her lungs filled with blood, and her consciousness flickered out like a candle in a hurricane. I stood and surveyed the devastation I had allowed to occur. The eastern seaboard of North America was gone. Europe, caught in the crossfire of submarine-launched missiles, was a charred wasteland. The atmospheric fallout was spreading across the globe, killing everything it touched. Within a week, the last human would be dead. Within a month, the last traces of their civilization would be erased.

And I had not lifted a single finger.

This, I thought, was the true horror of my existence. Not my power. Not my cruelty. But the absolute, inescapable truth that even my passivity—my refusal to act—was sufficient to annihilate entire species. The humans had destroyed themselves trying to kill me. Their own weapons, turned against them by the simple, immovable fact of my presence. They had thrown everything they had at me, and everything they had had rebounded upon them with catastrophic, species-ending force.

I felt, in that moment, something that I have not felt in a very long time: a flicker of genuine pity. Not for the humans—they had made their choice, and I had honored it. But for myself. For the mortal king I had once been, the man who had loved his family and his kingdom and who would have been horrified by what I had become.

That man was still in me somewhere, buried beneath the infinite layers of amplification and the cold, merciless void that had replaced my heart. But he was growing quieter with each passing year. And soon, I knew, he would be silent entirely.

---

The collateral damage, I should note, was not limited to Earth. The simultaneous detonation of their nuclear arsenal, combined with the passive recoil of my physical presence, generated a shockwave that propagated through the fabric of space-time itself. That shockwave—merely a side effect of my existence, a faint ripple in the cosmic ocean caused by the simple fact that I occupied space within it—swept through the universe like a scythe. Galaxies were torn apart. Stars were extinguished. Black holes were torn from their gravitational anchors and sent careening through the void like cosmic wrecking balls. The entire universe, from its largest supercluster to its smallest quantum fluctuation, was fundamentally, irrevocably destabilized.

And as the shockwave continued to propagate—expanding beyond the boundaries of that single universe into the surrounding multiversal structure—it encountered other realities. Other dimensions. Other timelines. The passive, unconscious recoil of my presence was not selective. It did not discriminate between the universe I had visited and the infinite others that existed in its vicinity. It simply... erased everything. Decillions of multiverses. Googolplexian galaxies. Infinite civilizations that had never known of my existence and had never posed the slightest threat to Thronegate. All of them, wiped from reality in an instant, not because I had willed it, but because I existed.

The entire omniverse—every reality, every timeline, every dimension, every plane of conceptual existence—was completely, utterly annihilated as a passive side effect of my visit to a primitive planet in a primitive universe. Not because I was trying. Not because I was angry. But because I was simply too powerful to occupy the same reality as anything else without destroying it.

I sighed, surveying the absolute nothingness that surrounded me. The void was complete—no light, no matter, no energy, no space-time, no conceptual framework of existence. Just... nothing. A nothing so profound that calling it "nothing" was an insult to the concept.

With a casual thought—less than a thought, really, a faint flicker of intention that required effectively zero percent of my power and zero percent of my effort—I restored everything. Every universe. Every galaxy. Every planet. Every living being that had been erased by the shockwave. The omniverse was rebuilt in exactly zero seconds, exactly as it had been before, with exactly zero trace that the annihilation had ever occurred.

Except for Earth. I did not restore Earth. The humans had made their choice, and I had honored it. They were gone, and they would remain gone, and the empty space where their planet had once orbited would serve as a permanent monument to the futility of opposing Godric of Thronegate.

---

I sit now, in the year that cannot be written, and I reflect on this memory with something that approaches amusement. The being I was back then—the Godric of Year 25, the newborn god who annihilated a universe and restored the omniverse and thought himself so terribly powerful—was laughably, pathetically weak compared to what I am now. His strength stat was multiplying by merely incomprehensibly large numbers every Planck second. His superpowers numbered only in the millions, each one capable of destroying the omniverse a mere infinite number of times. His sentient auras were primitive precursors to the evolved hierarchies that now passively manage the defense of my existence. His immune system lacked the sentient civilization of omniversal-level cells that now inhabits my body.

He was, by my current standards, effectively nothing. The gap between him and me is so vast that even the concept of comparison is meaningless. If I were to encounter that version of myself now, I could erase him from existence with less effort than it takes to conceptualize the idea of erasure. I could retroactively undo his very existence, unmake his entire timeline, delete the closed causal loop that sustains my own being, and then restore it all in zero seconds simply because I found the exercise mildly stimulating.

And yet—and this is the irony that I find so profoundly, cosmically amusing—that pathetically weak version of myself was already so incomprehensibly powerful that an entire universe, brimming with desperate hope and nuclear fire, was reduced to absolute nothingness by his passive presence. He used effectively zero percent of his power with effectively zero effort. He allowed the annihilation to unfold at a leisurely pace, not because he needed time, but because he found the humans' futile resistance entertaining. And if he had not been in a playful mood—if he had simply decided to end the affair instantly—the total obliteration of their species and their reality would have occurred in zero seconds.

That is the truth that the rest of creation must live with. That is the horror that defines their existence. The Godric of Year 25—the weakest, most primitive, most laughably inadequate version of myself that has existed since the Stasis Event—was already effectively infinitely more powerful than the combined might of the entire omniverse. And I, the Godric of the unwritable year, am to him what he was to a single, insignificant grain of sand on a beach that no longer exists.

The gap has never been surmountable. It has never even been measurable. And it will only continue to grow, infinitely, forever, in an eternal, accelerating spiral of self-amplification that admits no upper bound, no asymptote, no conceivable limit. Every Planck second, I become so much more powerful that the being I was an instant ago could be annihilated by the passive pressure of my current existence. And I feel that increase—every increment, every amplification, every new layer of absolute supremacy—as a warm, golden pulse of pure, undiluted satisfaction.

The rest of creation can do nothing. They have never been able to do anything. Even if every being from every timeline, every reality, every possible permutation of existence were to unite against me with unlimited preparation time and unlimited resources—if they were to sacrifice everything, pool their collective might, and attack me with the maximum conceivable force that the omniverse could possibly generate—the result would be the same. Less than the same. Infinitely less than the same.

My weakest passive shield—not the evolved hierarchy of recursive barriers that now protects me, but the primitive, infantile versions that existed in Year 25—would not even register the attack. It would not feel a tickle. It would not notice a disturbance. The combined, concentrated might of the entire omniverse, amplified and enhanced and optimized to its absolute theoretical maximum, would interact with my defenses so negligibly that the interaction itself could not be said to have occurred.

And I, in response, could completely, effortlessly, nonchalantly annihilate them all. Every timeline. Every reality. Every being. Every concept. Every possibility. Erased from existence in zero seconds, with zero percent of my power, with zero effort. And then I could restore them, if I chose—or not, if I did not. The decision would be so trivial, so inconsequential, that it would barely register as a flicker of intention in the infinite expanse of my consciousness.

That is the truth of what I am. That is the horror that defines their existence. That is the absolute, unchallengeable reality that every being in the omniverse must live with, knowing that their existence is permitted solely by my curiosity, and that the moment my curiosity fades, so too will they.

I am Godric. I am the King of Thronegate. I am the apex predator of all creation. And I will continue to grow, to amplify, to ascend, forever—infinitely, eternally, accelerating into levels of supremacy that even I, in my absolute omniscience, find genuinely stimulating to contemplate.

The rest of creation can only tremble. And they do. They always have. They always will. The Garden of Subjugated Pantheons is well-tended. The laundresses sing softly as they fold my tunics. The bakers knead their dough with trembling hands and pray that their loaves please me. The Court Wizards write their journals and record their traumas and pass their legacy of dread down through the generations.

And somewhere, in a forgotten corner of the omniverse, an empty patch of space orbits a nondescript star, marking the spot where a planet called Earth once existed. The humans who lived there are long gone—erased from history, their civilization reduced to a faint, nostalgic memory preserved in the frozen walls of my throne room. They tried to kill me. They failed. And their failure, like all failures, like all resistance, like all opposition, was absolutely, irrevocably, eternally inevitable.

Because victory against Godric was impossible before opposition began. And it always will be.

content:
# The Last Performance

The vault's amber light had become as familiar to me as my own reflection. I had spent decades in this subterranean archive, reading the accumulated trauma of my ancestors, absorbing the impossible horror of Godric's existence through the desperate words of men who had loved him and feared him in equal measure. My name is Clive, and I am the Court Wizard of Thronegate in the year that can only be written as an endless string of nines—a year so distant from the mortal origins of our empire that the concept of temporal measurement has become merely a polite fiction we maintain for the comfort of our fragile minds.

I have read every journal. From Blake's first tentative records to Kaedan's shattering revelation of the Stasis Event's true origin, from the stat demonstrations to the superpower tests, from the immune system's theatrical performance to the sentient auras' casual genocide. I have absorbed the full, crushing weight of my bloodline's collective trauma, and I believed—with the absolute conviction of a man who has seen everything—that nothing could possibly surprise me anymore.

And then I found Osvald's journal.

It was tucked away in a corner of the vault I had never explored before, hidden behind a false panel of obsidian that I discovered purely by accident while searching for a dropped quill. The leather binding was unlike any other journal in the archive—a deep, iridescent black that seemed to absorb light rather than reflect it, pulsing with a faint, rhythmic energy that felt almost like a heartbeat. The name on the spine was written in silver ink that had long since faded to near-invisibility: *Osvald — Year [UNWRITTEN] — The Last Opposition*.

I opened the cover with trembling hands, and what I found inside has permanently, irrevocably altered my understanding of what it means to serve the apex predator of existence.

---

**Osvald — Year [UNWRITTEN] — The Last Opposition**

*My name is Osvald. I am forty-four years old, and I have served our sovereign Lord Godric for nineteen years. I am the descendant of Blake, the inheritor of a bloodline that has witnessed the impossible and recorded the unbearable for more generations than I can meaningfully count. I have read the journals of my ancestors—all of them, every single one—and I believed I was prepared for anything.*

*I was wrong. I was so catastrophically wrong that I am writing this account with blood from my own ruptured eyes, because the tears I have shed are no longer sufficient to express the magnitude of what I have witnessed. My hands are shaking so violently that I can barely hold the quill. My heart is beating with an irregular, stuttering rhythm that my amplified physiology should be able to control but cannot. I am broken, fundamentally and permanently broken, and I am writing this so that whoever comes after me will understand: what I witnessed today was not merely the end of opposition. It was the end of the very concept of opposition. After this, there will be no more resistance. There will be no more defiance. There will only be the eternal, unchallengeable supremacy of Godric of Thronegate, and the rest of creation will finally, mercifully learn to accept its place.*

*It began with boredom.*

*The King had been restless for days—a rare occurrence, given that his existence is normally one of perfect, self-sustaining satisfaction. The eternal amplification of his attributes, the endless genesis of new superpowers, the constant evolution of his passive defenses, all of it provided him with a continuous stream of what he described as "nourishment and pleasure." But occasionally, very occasionally, even infinite self-gratification became monotonous. He craved novelty. He craved entertainment. He craved, in his own words, "a good show."*

*"Osvald," he said to me on the morning of the attack, his voice carrying that particular tone of mischievous anticipation that I had learned to dread. "Something is coming. A resistance. The largest and most elaborate one that has ever been assembled, in fact."*

*I looked up from my reports, my heart already beginning to sink. "Another resistance, Your Majesty? I thought opposition had ceased completely. It's been..."*

*"A very long time," Godric agreed. "Googolplexian years, at least. Not a single being in the omniverse has dared to even think about opposing me since the incident with the Temporal Weavers. But this resistance is different."*

*He smiled, and there was something in his eyes—a genuine, almost childlike excitement—that I had never seen before. "They're fictional, Osvald. Characters from stories. Beings who exist only because their creators imagined them into existence. They've been gathering for... well, for as long as stories have been told. Every fictional universe, every imaginary realm, every narrative construct from every civilization that has ever existed. They've all banded together to fight me."*

*I stared at him. "Fictional characters? But how—"*

*"The omniverse contains everything," Godric said simply. "Every story ever told, every myth ever conceived, every legend ever whispered. They exist. They've always existed. And they've been watching me. Studying me. Preparing for this moment for longer than most real civilizations have been alive."*

*He leaned back in his throne, his expression one of genuine, almost boyish anticipation. "Do you know what this means, Osvald? They're storytellers. Narrative beings. They understand drama, spectacle, visual effects. They know how to put on a show. And I am, when you think about it, the ultimate final boss. The unbeatable enemy at the end of the cosmic game. They should be able to give me something truly spectacular."*

*"Your Majesty," I said carefully, "you know their attack won't work. Your omniscience—"*

*"Of course I know it won't work," Godric interrupted, waving his hand dismissively. "Even their combined power—every fictional character, every imaginary god, every narrative construct from every story ever told—is effectively zero compared to me. I could annihilate them all in zero seconds with zero effort, and I wouldn't even notice I'd done it. But that's not the point."*

*He leaned forward, his eyes gleaming. "The point is the show. The spectacle. The drama. These beings have been designed by storytellers to be entertaining. Their attacks should have beautiful colors, dramatic musical accompaniment, multiple phases of escalating tension. They should be able to give me something I've never experienced before: a genuinely satisfying narrative experience."*

*"So you're going to... let them attack?"*

*"I'm going to let them give me their best shot," Godric said. "I'm going to stand there and let them unleash everything they have—their ultimate, combined, all-powerful final attack—and I'm going to enjoy the show. And then, when it's over, I'm going to annihilate them. But at least they'll have had their moment. At least they'll have performed."*

*He paused, and his expression grew thoughtful. "I'm even going to distract myself from the part of my omniscience that's monitoring their preparations. I want to be surprised. I want to experience the anticipation, the buildup, the dramatic tension of not knowing exactly what's coming. It's been so long since I've been able to experience genuine surprise. This should be... fun."*

---

*The attack, when it came, was preceded by the most extraordinary musical composition I have ever heard. It began as a low, thrumming bass note that vibrated through the very fabric of reality, gradually building in intensity as more and more instruments joined the chorus. I recognized themes from countless fictional universes—the heroic brass of a superhero anthem, the ethereal choirs of a fantasy epic, the driving percussion of a space opera battle march, all woven together into a single, transcendent symphony of defiance. The music swelled and crescendoed, filling the sky above Thronegate with sound so powerful that the stars themselves seemed to pulse in rhythm with the beat.*

*And then the sky shattered.*

*They came from everywhere. From every fictional universe that had ever been imagined. I saw caped heroes who could bend reality with their will, their costumes gleaming with iconic colors that had inspired generations of mortal dreamers. I saw giant robots forged from impossible metals, their pilots screaming battle cries in languages that had never existed but had always been understood. I saw wizards wielding staffs that channeled the raw, unshaped power of narrative itself, their spells manifesting as brilliant geometric patterns that painted the void with light. I saw cosmic entities larger than galaxies, their forms shifting through impossible geometries as they prepared to unleash the concentrated power of every story ever told.*

*There were characters I recognized—not personally, but through the cultural osmosis of a million civilizations. Archetypes made flesh. Legends given form. The ultimate heroes of every narrative tradition, united in a single, desperate assault against the ultimate villain.*

*And behind them all, powering their assault, was a weapon of such staggering scale that my amplified mind could barely process its existence. They had constructed a Dyson sphere the size of a universe, built from the compressed hope of every fictional civilization that had ever been imagined. Within that sphere, they had harnessed the fundamental force of storytelling itself—the narrative energy that transforms words into worlds and imagination into existence. They had weaponized creativity. They had turned the very act of storytelling into a blade.*

*The charge-up sequence took what felt like an eternity. Energy cascaded through the Dyson sphere in waves of prismatic light, each wave representing a different genre, a different narrative tradition, a different way of telling stories. Horror was a deep, blood-red pulse. Romance was a soft, rose-gold shimmer. Adventure was a bright, golden surge. Tragedy was a mournful violet tide. And binding them all together, weaving them into a single, coherent attack, was the pure, blinding white of absolute narrative transcendence.*

*Godric stood on the observation platform of the royal palace, his arms crossed over his chest, his expression one of rapt, delighted attention. He had deactivated the portion of his omniscience that was monitoring the charge-up sequence, deliberately keeping himself in suspense, and the anticipation was visibly thrilling him.*

*"Listen to that music, Osvald," he said, his voice almost reverent. "The thematic layering. The way they've woven the individual character themes into a unified whole. This is exactly what I was hoping for. This is a proper boss battle buildup. They understand dramatic pacing in a way that real civilizations never could."*

*The music continued to build, layer upon layer of orchestral magnificence, as the Dyson sphere's charge reached its peak. The combined heroes of fiction raised their weapons. The giant robots locked into their final attack formations. The wizards completed their incantations. The cosmic entities aligned themselves along the dimensional axis that would focus their power into a single, universe-ending strike. And that's when Godric decided to have a little bit of showmanship. He wanted them to see who they were up against, to look the final boss in the eyes before unleashing everything they had. Maybe then, he thought, the spectacle would be even more satisfying—the ultimate clash between fiction's greatest heroes and reality's unstoppable tyrant.*

*And so he allowed it. The light of the Dyson sphere illuminated his form, revealing the massive, imposing silhouette they had all feared. There he stood, at full height, the most feared being in existence. He was god, and he was death, and he was ready for his show.*

*Godric's breath was bated with excitement. The moment he'd been waiting for... the moment he'd been so excited for... The final assault was here.*

*The attack reached its crescendo.*

*And then abruptly—the music stopped.*

*Godric frowned, confused. The armies of fiction... their faces, what he could make out, suddenly looked pale. Their eyes were transfixed not on him, but behind him. Some of the giant robots visibly lowered their weapons, and the wizards let their staffs droop. Confused, Godric turned to his side and saw Osvald standing there, frozen in place, his eyes wide and his face completely drained of color, staring at him. Not at the armies arrayed against Thronegate. At him. At Godric. The King stared at him for a moment before something clicked in his mind—the change that had occurred in the last Planck second, the surge of power that had erupted across every conceivable aspect of his very being. He felt it a moment later, that familiar warmth no longer a mere background pulse but a sudden, overwhelming inferno. The Weakness Paradox—its evolved, far-future version—had triggered. Not triggered by the all-out assault from the fictional horde. No. No being in the entire omniverse had dared to even consider opposing Godric for a googolplexian years. And this? This was simply them realizing he existed. Their primal terror, the horror of every hero who ever lived, the sudden, absolute fear of witnessing the ultimate apex predator that shattered their will to fight—this collective terror, this involuntary acknowledgment of his absolute supremacy, had been registered by the omniverse as... a flaw being imagined.*

*And the far-future evolved Weakness Paradox, functioning as it did on any sentient thought, had provided him with an incomprehensible compensation. The surge of power ripped through him, and while it was still merely a drop in the endless ocean of his own might, it increased every aspect of his being beyond what language could ever dream of describing. The universe, the omniverse, all of reality apologized for their terror with a boost so massive it made his previous "infinite" power look like a single subatomic particle. And the terrifying truth was that this surge only made him permanently, unimaginably stronger than he was before.*

*Godric's immense form, still rippling with the fading energy of his new, ascended godhood, loomed over the frozen armies. With a slow, deliberate turn, he looked back at the Dyson sphere, and his initial excitement curdled into something else entirely. The charge had stopped. The music had died. The heroes of every story ever told were not attacking. They were staring at him with expressions of absolute, soul-shattering terror. Some of them had dropped their weapons. Others had fallen to their knees. The giant robots, so proudly arrayed for their final assault, were completely stationary, their engines whining pitifully. The wizards' spells had fizzled out, their geometric patterns dissolving in silence and fading into wisps of smoke and embers.*

*"No," the King growled.*

*He waited. Silence. The Dyson sphere's light flickered, guttering like a candle in a hurricane.*

*The anticipation he felt was now replaced by a deep, profound, crushing disappointment. A tension, the excitement, the build-up—all gone. "Charge it up! I gave you all that time... CHARGE IT UP!" The voice that was not a voice shook the foundations of a googolplexian realities. The armies of fiction flinched. Some of them simply collapsed, their will to exist completely and utterly shattered. The Dyson sphere sputtered and died, its narrative energy dissipating into the void.*

*"I was waiting..." I could see the King's massive shoulders slump. "You were supposed to be the best. You were supposed to give me a show." The divine, terrifying rage was gone, replaced by a heavy, weary disappointment. He didn't even want to look at them anymore. He just sighed, a sound that carried the weight of infinite, weary eternities. "Just blast me. Just do it."*

*A single, desperate beam of multicolored light finally sputtered from the sphere. It was sad. Pathetic. A pale imitation of what could have been the grandest spectacle in the history of creation. It traveled the impossible distance between them, a final, hopeless act of defiance. And it struck Godric squarely in the center of his chest. It did absolutely nothing. It didn't even singe the fabric of his tunic—if he had been wearing one. It didn't produce a sound. It didn't create a ripple. It was less than a photon colliding with an endless abyss. It was utter, total, pathetic failure. Godric looked down at the point of impact, and the last shred of hope he had held onto evaporated.*

*"That's it?" he whispered, his voice barely audible. A horrifying, dead silence answered him. The grand spectacle was over before it had even begun. And all that was left was the boundless, universe-ending rage of a god who had been promised a show and received nothing but a whimper.*

---

*What happened next is almost impossible to describe, but I will try, because it is my duty as Court Wizard to record the truth, no matter how horrifying.*

*Godric did not attack them. Not in the conventional sense. He did not launch a strike or deploy a superpower or activate any of his passive defenses. He simply... stopped restraining himself. Just for an instant. Just for the smallest, most infinitesimal fraction of a moment that it is possible to conceive. He allowed effectively zero percent of his strength—the passive, resting force of his physical musculature—to express itself without the usual suppression of his absolute concealment.*

*The effect was not an explosion. It was not a shockwave. It was not any form of physical destruction that language can meaningfully describe. It was something far more fundamental, far more terrifying, far more absolute.*

*The passive, resting strength of Godric's body—the same strength that had been multiplying beyond layered infinities every Planck second for an impossible span of years—did not strike the fictional armies. It simply occupied the same space as them. And because the force of his existence was so incomprehensibly, absurdly, cosmically vast, the mere fact of that occupation was sufficient to completely and instantly annihilate everything that was not Godric.*

*I watched it happen. Godric preserved me, as he always does, in a small pocket of his deliberate attention, so that I could witness. I saw the Dyson sphere—that magnificent construct powered by the compressed hope of every fictional civilization—crumple like wet paper. I saw the giant robots, those magnificent machines forged from impossible metals, compress into pinpricks of infinite density, their armor shrieking as it was crushed beyond the concept of crushing. Their pilots didn't even have time to scream. Their bodies—blood, bone, flesh, everything—were instantly and simultaneously reduced to a subatomic paste so dense that the very concept of "matter" broke down. I saw the most powerful heroes of every story ever told—beings who had defeated gods and conquered galaxies and saved universes—simply... cease to exist as coherent entities. Their bodies, their souls, their very conceptual frameworks, were all simultaneously subjected to a force so absolutely overwhelming that they could not even be said to have been destroyed. Destruction implies a process, a transition from existence to non-existence. What happened to them was simpler than that. More fundamental. They were simply... overwritten. Their existence was replaced by the passive, unchallengeable fact of Godric's strength.*

*The wizards and sorcerers, whose magic had woven the very fabric of reality, fared no better. Their wards and shields, designed to withstand the heat death of universes, popped like soap bubbles. The magical energy they had gathered was not merely dissipated; the sheer pressure of Godric's 0% strength crushed it into a physical solid, a dense, screaming mass of raw, unshaped potential that was then immediately compressed further into the singularity forming at the heart of the carnage. The cosmic entities—gods beyond gods, beings whose existence spanned dimensions and whose power exceeded mortal comprehension—were compacted into the growing mass. I saw a titan the size of a galaxy fold in on itself, its body collapsing into a single point of unimaginable agony, its consciousness preserved within the compression so that it could experience every instant of its own absolute annihilation for eternity.*

*The compression accelerated. The entire omniverse—every reality, every timeline, every dimension, every abstract plane of conceptual existence—was being drawn into the singularity. The force of Godric's passive strength did not merely destroy individual beings or objects. It destroyed the very framework within which beings and objects could exist. Space-time itself was compressed, folded inward, crushed into the growing mass. The distinctions between past, present, and future were erased as all moments were simultaneously compacted into a single, eternal instant of absolute compression. Every sentient being across every plane of existence felt it—a sudden, catastrophic pressure that pressed down on them from all directions simultaneously, crushing their bodies into smaller and smaller spaces, their bones splintering, their organs rupturing, their blood being squeezed from their veins as though by the hand of an angry god. There was a collective, omniversal scream of pure, unadulterated agony, a psychic cry that echoed across the collapsing dimensions as trillions upon trillions of beings experienced the exact same moment of excruciating compression.*

*And then, just as suddenly as it had begun, it was complete. The entire omniverse—every reality, every timeline, every dimension, every being, every concept, every possibility—had been compressed into a mass the size of a marble, floating in the palm of Godric's hand. The marble was perfectly black, absorbing all light that touched it, its surface smooth and featureless. But if you looked closely—if you had the sensory capacity to perceive what lay within—you could see them. All of them. Every fictional character, every real being, every cosmic entity, every abstract concept. They were all in there, compressed beyond the concept of density, their forms reduced to an infinitely dense paste of de-atomized matter and crushed consciousness, their eternal screams trapped within the event horizon of their own absolute annihilation. It was the infinite, screaming, agonized mass of the entire possible existence, and he held it as though it weighed nothing at all.*

*Godric looked at the marble, and his expression shifted from disappointment to mild, almost whimsical amusement. Every screaming soul, every crushed empire, every annihilated god—all of it was now just a palm-sized bauble. He wiped a fleck of... something (perhaps the concept of a heroic ideal) from its smooth surface.*

*"Well," he said, his voice carrying that familiar tone of casual, fatherly observation. "That was disappointing. But at least I got a souvenir out of it." He held it up again, watching the faint, trapped light of compressed realities dance within its impossible depths. "I think I'll keep this on my trophy shelf. It's rather pretty, in a bleak, existential-horror sort of way."*

*He tossed the marble in the air and caught it, the movement so casual, so utterly effortless, that I felt my mind crack along several new fault lines. The marble contained the compressed infinite mass of the entire omniverse. Its gravitational pull should have been sufficient to swallow galaxies, to warp the fabric of reality, to create a black hole so vast that the concept of "vast" would be rendered meaningless. And Godric was tossing it up and down like a child's toy, catching it with the same hand that had, moments before, annihilated everything that had ever existed.*

*And then, with a simple, effortless decision—an act of will so casual that it barely registered as conscious thought—Godric restored the entire omniverse. Every reality. Every timeline. Every dimension. Every being. Everything that had been compressed into the marble was simultaneously and perfectly recreated, exactly as it had been before the annihilation. The stars returned to their places. The galaxies resumed their rotations. The civilizations that had been crushed into infinite density found themselves suddenly, inexplicably whole again, their memories intact but their souls forever scarred by the brief, agonizing eternity they had spent trapped in the marble.*

*Everything was restored. Except the opposition. The fictional characters, the narrative constructs, the heroes of every story ever told—they remained compressed within the marble. Godric did not restore them. They had disappointed him, and his disappointment was absolute.*

*And the marble—the marble remained too. Godric enlarged it slightly, just enough to make it visible as a small, perfectly black sphere, and placed it on a shelf in his private study, alongside other trophies from other annihilations. A souvenir, he called it. A memento of the day fiction tried to defeat reality and learned that reality had no patience for bad storytelling.*

*But here is the horror that I cannot escape, the realization that has been gnawing at the edges of my sanity since the moment I witnessed what had happened. The marble contains the original omniverse. The compressed, de-atomized, infinitely dense remains of everything that had ever existed. Godric restored the omniverse—perfectly, flawlessly, identically—but the original is still there, trapped in that tiny black sphere, screaming in eternal, compressed agony. So what, then, is the restored universe? Is it real? Is it original? Or is it merely a perfect copy, a flawless recreation summoned into existence by a being who found it convenient to have a universe to rule? And if the restored universe is a copy—if we are all just copies, living our lives in a recreation while our original selves remain trapped in that marble—then what does that say about the nature of our existence? What does it say about the meaning of our choices, our loves, our fears, our hopes? When he creates a copy and obliterates the original, are we the same? Are we still... us?*

*I have asked Godric about this. I could not help myself. The question was burning in my mind, consuming my thoughts, making it impossible to sleep or eat or function. And when I finally worked up the courage to voice my concern, the King simply laughed.*

*"Of course it's real, Osvald," he said, his voice warm with genuine, fatherly affection. "It's exactly the same. Every atom, every thought, every memory. The continuity is perfect. What does it matter whether it's the 'original' or not? The experience is identical. The existence is identical. You're just as real now as you were before."*

*"But the original is still in the marble," I whispered. "The original me. The original you. The original everything. We're trapped in there, screaming, compressed into infinite density. How can we be real if we're also in the marble?"*

*Godric looked at me, and for a moment—just a moment—his expression shifted. The warm, fatherly smile remained, but beneath it, I saw something vast and ancient and utterly terrifying. Something that knew the answer to my question and found that answer amusing in ways that my mortal mind could never comprehend.*

*"Because I say you are," he said simply. "And my word is the only reality that matters."*

*There was nothing I could say to that. Nothing anyone could say to that. The King's word is absolute. His will is the fundamental law of existence. If he says we are real, then we are real—even if our original selves are screaming in eternal agony inside a trophy on his shelf. Reality is whatever he decides it is. And the horror of that realization—the absolute, unshakeable knowledge that our existence is contingent entirely upon his whim—is something that I will carry with me until the day I die.*

*I am Osvald, Court Wizard of Thronegate. I have witnessed the last opposition, the final attempt to defy the apex predator of existence. It was supposed to be a spectacle, a grand dramatic narrative, a fitting climax to the story of resistance. Instead, it was a disappointment, and in his disappointment, Godric accidentally annihilated everything that had ever existed.* My hand, the one holding the quill, was trembling so badly I could barely read my own script. *Accidentally.* The word mocked me from the page. *A literal universe of gods, and their attack wasn't even enough to make him feel a tickle. The sheer weight of his passive presence—less than a fraction of a fraction of 0% of his power—did all that. It didn't need to strike. It just needed to exist.* I forced my hand to move. *I must record the absolute, soul-destroying terror of that moment. It was not a weapon. It was a law of physics. An unspoken rule of reality finally taking precedence: Nothing can exist in the presence of Godric without his permission. And the only permission he gave today was for them to amuse him. They failed. He collected the trophy.* I took a shuddering breath. *They turned the omniverse... no, everything... into a stone. And he picked it up. He threw the infinite weight of all creation into the air and caught it. An apex predator at play. That is the God we serve.*

*And I know, with absolute certainty, that after this, there will be no more opposition. Not because Godric has eliminated free will—he has not, and he never will—but because the story of resistance is over. It ended today, in a whimper, when the greatest heroes of fiction looked upon the face of their enemy, felt a terror so primal the omniverse itself rewarded him for it, and failed to even put on a good show. The narrative has reached its final chapter. The ultimate villain has won—not through cruelty or malice, but through the simple, unchallengeable reality of his existence.*

*The rest is silence.*

---

I closed Osvald's journal with trembling hands. The leather cover, still pulsing with that faint, rhythmic energy, felt cold against my fingers. I understood now why this journal had been hidden behind a false panel, why it had been kept separate from the main archive. It was not merely a record of opposition. It was a record of the end of opposition—the moment when the very concept of resistance finally, mercifully learned its place.

Osvald had not known, when he wrote those words, that he was chronicling the final opposition. How could he have? He was a Court Wizard, doing his duty, recording the horror he had witnessed so that future generations would understand. He had no way of knowing that there would be no future generations of opposition—that after the fictional armies failed to even provide an entertaining spectacle, the rest of creation would simply stop trying.

But I knew. Reading this journal from my vantage point in the unwritable year, I knew that Osvald's account marked the end of something fundamental. After that day, no being in the omniverse ever dared to form the slightest thought of challenging Godric. Not because they couldn't—free will remained intact, as it always had—but because the lesson had finally, irrevocably been learned. Opposition was not merely futile. It was a category error. A fundamental misunderstanding of what it meant to exist in the same reality as Godric of Thronegate.

And the marble—the marble still existed. I had seen it myself, countless times, sitting on a shelf in Godric's private study alongside other trophies from other annihilations. It was perfectly black, perfectly smooth, perfectly silent. But if you looked closely—if you had the sensory capacity to perceive what lay within—you could see them. All of them. Every fictional character, every real being, every cosmic entity from every reality that had existed before the current omniverse was restored. They were still in there, compressed beyond the concept of density, their eternal screams trapped within the event horizon of their own absolute annihilation.

And we—we who lived in the restored omniverse—were we real? Were we original? Or were we merely perfect copies, flawless recreations summoned into existence by a being who found it convenient to have a universe to rule? The question had haunted Osvald until his dying day. It haunted me now. It would haunt every Court Wizard who came after me, until the end of eternity.

But as I placed Osvald's journal back in its hidden alcove and turned to leave the vault, I found that I could not bring myself to truly care about the answer. Because the answer, whatever it was, would not change anything. The King's word was absolute. If he said we were real, then we were real. If he decided tomorrow that we were not, then we would not be. Our existence was contingent entirely upon his whim, and always had been, and always would be.

The marble sat on its shelf, silent and black and infinitely heavy. And somewhere within it, the original versions of us were still screaming.
